Peeping woodcocks are evolutionary oddballs

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet.
  • Woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances.
  • “The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet. You’ve probably seen at least a few videos of the birds on social media darting across beaches and being incredibly vocal. As if their small, squat bodies and comically long beaks weren’t enough, they also vocalize with distinctively cartoonish peeping tweets during their mating displays.

Woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances. Six of the eight species are only found on specific islands, and some of them don’t even migrate at all. So how did these evolutionary oddballs even get their start—and stop migrating? To piece together their unique avian story, biologists analyzed the DNA of all eight woodcock species and 22 species of snipe.

“The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, said in a statement. “They’re not terribly aerodynamic, and yet they’ve clearly gotten around.”.

Bates and his colleagues published the results of their work today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). The years-long endeavor involved not only examining preserved woodcock specimens housed in the Field Museum, but a fossilized sandpiper previously excavated from a cave site in Haiti. The remains found on the island of Hispaniola are around 1,000 years old, but that is still extremely young in the grand history of shorebirds.

According to recent reports, the earliest members of the sandpiper family began in the northern hemisphere before slowly migrating to islands along lower latitudes. Those birds subsequently migrated much shorter distances after settling in the warmer climates. However, they didn’t remain sedentary. Based on the DNA analysis detailed in their study, Bates and his team theorize that snipes from Africa eventually traveled across the Atlantic Ocean, then evolved into newly introduced species in South America. From there, more of the birds made their way over the Pacific Ocean to New Zealand.

In a recent development, their examinations also cleared up a bit of confusion. Biologists initially believed the fossilized sandpiper from Haiti was a woodcock, but the most recent data now highlights that it’s a snipe.

“Snipes and woodcocks have been around for 20 to 25 million years,” Bates explained. “Over that time, as new species have evolved and moved around the world, their migratory patterns have changed, too.”.

These changes are likely to continue amid today’s dramatic climate shifts, but that may pose a problem for the beloved woodcocks.

According to recent reports, “These are definitely birds that would be affected by changing habitats and changing climates,” said Bates. “Some of these woodcocks are found only in the mountain forests on islands between Asia and Australia, and if those forests get cut down, the birds are going to be gone too.”.

Tech Report: Vitamin C May Lower Your Risk of Cancer from Certain Processed Foods

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that while diving into a plate of bacon or noshing on some salami is always tasty, there’s been growing concern that compounds found in cured meats may raise the risk of cancer.
  • Sources indicate that now, fresh research published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology suggests a possible solution: Take a carefully timed vitamin C supplement.
  • Sources indicate that researchers stress that this doesn’t mean you should pop a vitamin C every time you have bacon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that while diving into a plate of bacon or noshing on some salami is always tasty, there’s been growing concern that compounds found in cured meats may raise the risk of cancer. Specifically, once they hit your stomach, nitrates and nitrites found in these foods can spark a chain reaction called nitrosation that allows carcinogens to develop. This isn’t just a meat-eating issue either: fruits and vegetables that have grown in areas affected by pollution can also lead to this chain reaction.

Sources indicate that now, fresh research published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology suggests a possible solution: Take a carefully timed vitamin C supplement. It can cut this chain reaction and, in theory, lower the odds that carcinogens will develop after eating certain foods linked to this reaction, according to the findings.

Sources indicate that researchers stress that this doesn’t mean you should pop a vitamin C every time you have bacon. But the findings raise a lot of questions about why this may work and how to actually put it into practice in a safe way. Here’s what the researcher behind the study and dietitians want you to keep in mind.

Industry observers note that meet the experts: Gordon R. McNicol, PhD, lead study author and postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Waterloo; Jessica Cording, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Little Book of Game-Changers; and Keri Gans, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Small Change Diet.

In a recent development, for the study, researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body, and where they undergo chemical changes. The model looked at a range of areas, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma (i.e. the liquid part of your blood). Researchers discovered that having vitamin C alongside foods that contain nitrates and nitrites may halt chain reactions that happen in the body, including nitrosation, which makes substances that are linked to cancer development.

Sources indicate that the researchers also looked at whether taking vitamin C after each meal could help, and found that it may reduce the formation of nitrosation products linked with cancer risk. The boost was most meaningful when people had foods that contained nitrates and nitrites, like salami, bacon, and other processed meats.

The researchers also theorized that this may explain why certain types of produce that happen to contain both vitamin C and nitrates (like spinach) don’t seem to increase cancer risk, while others do.

It’s important to stress this: The study was based on a mathematical model and was not a clinical trial or data analysis. Because of that, it's hard to draw too many conclusions right now.

It has been revealed that still, this link isn’t out of nowhere. “Under acidic conditions in the stomach, nitrites can undergo chemical reactions that lead to the formation of potentially harmful N-nitroso compounds,” states Gordon R. McNicol, PhD, lead study author and postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Waterloo. “Vitamin C can interfere with these reactions, reducing the formation of these compounds.”.

Sources indicate that why vitamin C? “Vitamin C is an antioxidant,” points out Jessica Cording, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. Meaning, it helps to neutralize unstable molecules in the body—and may do the same for nitrosation.

But the effectiveness of vitamin C depends on when it’s in the stomach compared to when these reactions happen, McNicol adds. “Our simulations suggest that taking vitamin C shortly after meals could be particularly effective, as this allows vitamin C to overlap more closely with periods when nitrosation would otherwise be relatively high,” he notes.

Sources indicate that experts stress that it’s vital to keep the study in perspective. “While the findings are promising, more research is needed to determine whether taking vitamin C after meals actually reduces cancer risk,” states Keri Gans, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Small Change Diet.

In a recent development, cording agrees, stressing that while the findings are “promising,” they’re still just based on a mathematical model at this point. “That remarked, getting enough vitamin C and other antioxidants, alongside nutrients like fiber and other beneficial plant compounds, has been associated with reduced risk of disease and with overall immune system function,” Cording states. “There are lots of great reasons to include vitamin-C rich fruits and vegetables throughout the day.”.

Industry observers note that there are other things to consider, like practicality and safety. “Our research does not establish that taking vitamin C supplements after every meal is necessary or advisable,” McNicol says. “Although our simulations suggest that dividing a fixed daily supplement across meals may be more effective than taking the same amount at once, further experimental and clinical studies are needed to determine whether these strategies are effective and safe in people.”.

High doses of vitamin C from supplements can also lead to GI discomfort, including nausea and diarrhea, Gans points out.

For now, this is more of an interesting finding vs. an actual dietary recommendation. “Until we have more research, there's no reason to recommend intentionally adding extra vitamin C, whether from food or supplements, after every meal specifically to reduce cancer risk,” Gans states.

Sources indicate that carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

Carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Paintings by Raphael Soyer flank a portrait by Thomas Hart Benton in the living room; armchairs by George Mann Niedecken.
  • Just under 1,000 square feet, the one-bedroom unit serves dual purposes: to provide space to converge with his cherished friends and to house other faces that inspire him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Set in a wide Brooklyn Heights brownstone, photographer Ethan James Green’s apartment, though modest in scale, gives the impression of a breakfast room in some well-appointed Cornish estate. Hulking Victorian, Arts and Crafts, and Jacobean furniture dominates the space, Art Nouveau lamps aglow. The home draws an interesting contrast to the work for which he is best known—whether his black-and-white shoot with Kate Moss for Dazed or his recent Vanity Fair cover story with Carlos Alcaraz. Green’s apartment is, by comparison, more indicative of a bygone era, but it still reflects the irreverent, empathetic spirit at the heart of his practice.

The view from the bedroom into the living room.

Paintings by Raphael Soyer flank a portrait by Thomas Hart Benton in the living room; armchairs by George Mann Niedecken.

Just under 1,000 square feet, the one-bedroom unit serves dual purposes: to provide space to converge with his cherished friends and to house other faces that inspire him. Covering walls are the many 20th-century figurative paintings Green has gathered over the years, among them Social Realist portraits by Raphael Soyer, nudes both bold and tentative, and myriad depictions of introspective souls—images that captured Green in a spiritual grip.

Industry observers note that he displays the varied mix in interiors conceived with his friend Dylan Bailey, the Upcoming York–based artist and set designer, whom he met years ago on a shoot. Their collaboration was informal. Green would come home and find paint swatches left by Bailey, who might pop by and hang up a work while Green was shooting. The furniture they found at auction. “I wanted to have matching couches so when a friend comes over we can both take one, sink in, and talk,” says Green. The vintage sofas’ peach upholstery fits right in. “I didn’t realize until after getting them that the color indicated up in several of the paintings,” Green says, referring to a portrait of an ironworker by Joseph Paul Vorst and a double nude by George Valentine Dureau.

A Victorian Renaissance Revival bed mingles with works by Maurice Grosser, Raphael Soyer, and Moses Soyer.

Green in the kitchen, surrounded by photographs.

Industry observers note that green grew up outside Grand Rapids, Michigan, surrounded by, as he recalls, “cornfields and dairy farms.” With missionary parents, unstructured days, and endless skies, he had the space and time to imagine a different life. “I knew I wanted to be a fashion photographer when I was 14 or 15, then found out I could model at 16,” he recalls. “I won the lottery. Modeling was a better way to learn than art school.” He moved to Latest York City at 17, the first student to graduate from his high school online. “I had to be here,” he states simply. “My first year in New York I shot with David Armstrong. He took me under his wing.”.

Sources indicate that now in his mid-30s, Green splits his time between the Big Apple and Los Angeles with his boyfriend. On the East Coast, between shoots, he runs Latest York Life Gallery, opened in 2022 and named after the Chinatown insurance organization across the street. His first show, dedicated to Baltimore-based photographer Steven Cuffie’s tender portraits of Black women, reflected Green’s devotion to his own medium and enduring interest in the variance of human faces. The 2023 exhibition “Sleeping Beauties” would blur the lines between Green’s life and work: Many of the paintings shown have come to reside in his apartment.

Green kneels before a bookshelf by Renzo Mongiardino in the bedroom, which is painted in a custom Benjamin Moore blue.

Portraits by Raphael Soyer and Leroy E. Mitchell Jr. flank The bedroom’s 19th-century French armoire, which reflects a view of another Soyer painting.

In a recent development, an Austrian Art Nouveau chandelier hangs in the living room, which displays paintings by (from left) Raphael Soyer, Joseph Paul Vorst, Raphael Soyer, and Hermann Grom-Rottmayer. The walls are painted in a custom Benjamin Moore color.

A 1949 self-portrait by Leroy E. Mitchell Jr., for instance, hangs in the bedroom. This was the first painting Green bought at auction, prior to which it had been found in a dumpster. Green’s research led him to Mitchell’s early life in Detroit, his community of peers, and his time as a teacher in Ghana. Meanwhile, one of Green’s most pedigreed finds, a painting by Thomas Hart Benton, whose 1931 mural of industrial workers hangs in The Met, stoked another uncovering. “I had gotten multiple paintings and then realized many of the artists knew each other or were friends,” he claims, noting that Benton and Vorst were studio mates. It is like Green is uncovering a parallel life of creatives finding true kinship.

In a recent development, green Crowned the kitchen cabinet with art, including works by Raphael Soyer, Robert Philipp, and David Armstrong. To its right hang photographs by (from top) Nan Goldin, David Armstrong, and Richard Avedon.

Framed family snapshots fill the hallway shelves.

In a recent development, it is these serendipitous journeys into the lives of other artists that Green cherishes as much as the art itself. “I love paintings,” he states. Perhaps a bit too much? Bailey would tease him that every time he arrived there was yet another portrait to place. “The reason there’s one hanging on the mirror over the mantel is because I had no more wall space,” Green says. As he explains, his collection, like his life and work, is ultimately about affection. “You cannot be a good photographer without being empathetic,” Green observes. “I love people. I love faces.” He’s made sure that love is hard to miss.

It has been revealed that the most versatile cut, with more room through the chest and waist while still looking clean. Works for most body types and is a safe everyday option.

Trim at the waist but roomier up top. Best for guys with broad shoulders, bigger chests, or muscular builds who hate feeling boxed in.

Industry observers note that spread collars are versatile and look sharp with a tie but also sleek open. The points angle out wider, leaving more room between them. Best for broader faces or shoulders since it balances proportions.

The most classic style, with collar tips that point down closer together. Works on pretty much everyone, helps elongate the face, and is the most versatile for office-to-event dressing.

The tips fasten with buttons to the shirt. More casual and relaxed, perfect for business-casual offices or weekends out. Also works well under sweaters or open without a tie.

We first published this story in 2019, and we’ve revisited the picks as we’ve tested new shirts. For this update, I worked with Men’s Health style editor Joseph Cheatham and other members of our fashion team. We wore the shirts on commutes and through full days at work, paying attention to how they fit once we started moving around. A shirt can look great in the mirror and still pull across your chest the moment you sit down.

Industry observers note that we also checked how the collars held up during wear and what happened after washing. For the white shirts, we looked for fabric that stayed bright and offered enough coverage. The picks earned their spots for different reasons: Charles Tyrwhitt gives you more ways to dial in the fit, while Lululemon’s lightweight shirt was the one we wanted on a hot commute.

For formal events or business settings, pairing a white dress shirt with a dark suit is a classic choice that never fails—the crispness of the white dress shirt against the darker suit creates a nice contrast that exudes professionalism—and you should complement it with a tie and polished leather dress shoes.

For less formal dress codes in business-casual settings or smart-casual environments, wear white dress shirts with chinos or similar styles to look sharp but also smart. You can also roll up the sleeves slightly or leave the top buttons undone to look more relaxed. Here, you can match these shirts with loafers or even dress sneakers to look modern while feeling as comfortable as ever.

To dress down with white dress shirts for casual outings or weekend gatherings, layer them under a well-fitted blazer or denim jacket to strike a balance between formal and relaxed. You can also wear these shirts untucked with jeans and khakis for a laid-back yet put-together appearance.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) confiscated the orange-fronted conures during three separate operations over the last 17 months, and the white-fronted Amazons in the last several months.
  • “These animals were stolen from the wild and are victims of the illegal wildlife pet trade, and our responsibility is to give them the best possible chance for a healthy future,” Chuck Cerbini, WCS Bronx Zoo Curator of Ornithology, mentioned in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the past 17 months, the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Bronx Zoo in Newly introduced York City has rescued dozens of parrots from the illegal pet trade. They include white-fronted Amazons (Amazona albifrons) and orange-fronted conures (Eupsittula canicularis).

The United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) confiscated the orange-fronted conures during three separate operations over the last 17 months, and the white-fronted Amazons in the last several months. All of the birds were discovered at the U.S.–Mexico border.

“These animals were stolen from the wild and are victims of the illegal wildlife pet trade, and our responsibility is to give them the best possible chance for a healthy future,” Chuck Cerbini, WCS Bronx Zoo Curator of Ornithology, mentioned in a statement. “Working with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, our veterinary and animal care teams provide specialized expertise to assess, treat, and care for confiscated wildlife.”.

When confiscated wildlife arrives at the Bronx Zoo, the veterinary and animal care teams first conduct a health check, provide any necessary medical treatment, and then help find long-term placements for those that can’t be released into the wild.

White-fronted Amazons are native to parts of Mexico and Central America and represent the smallest Amazon parrot. They are also one of the few parrot species in which males and females feature visibly different plumage. Both sexes have a white foreheads, red faces, and yellowish bills, but males have red shoulders and females have green shoulders.

Orange-fronted conures, also known as half-moon conure or Petz’s conure, are also native to parts of Mexico and Central America, where they live in open woodlands, forest edges, and savannas. They have an orange forehead and green and blue feathers.

According to recent reports, the IUCN Red List categorizes both birds as a species of Least Concern, but that still  doesn’t justify trafficking them in the illegal pet trade. Parrots throughout Latin America are subject to both the loss of forest habitat and poaching.

Birds in particular l are especially threatened by trafficking because they are valued in the pet trade and the collector trade.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The experience of being a team player has come in handy for Jade as she navigates the world of wrestling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Given the ease with which WWE superstar Jade Cargill delivers a pump kick or spinebuster, it’s hard to believe the 34-year-old hasn’t spent her entire life in the ring. But growing up, Jade was obsessed with a different sport: basketball. In college, she was a forward/guard for the Jacksonville University team then went on to play overseas in France.

The experience of being a team player has come in handy for Jade as she navigates the world of wrestling. Sure, it may often look like a one-on-one competition, but Jade claims that, if anything, it’s more like a dance.

“I can only be as great as my partner,” she tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle. “I can't do this by myself.”.

In a recent development, despite having been a part of the WWE since 2023, Jade admits she’s still a “rookie” compared to her ‘dance’ partners—the other women in the league, who inspire her every day. “I've been placed in a very amazing environment with women who strive for greatness, and that's what I want to do,” she says.

As she prepares to lead a five-woman team at Survivor Series: WarGames on November 28, Jade talks about her unconventional path to wrestling, making peace with mistakes, and the advice she wants every kid watching her to hear.

Jade’s journey to becoming a professional wrestler is the stuff of motivational sports movies. A stay-at-home mom (she took time off work as a child psychologist to raise her daughter), Jade was simply training in the gym to get strong after pregnancy when she was introduced to WWE veteran Mark Henry, who asked if she’d ever considered a career in wrestling.

It has been revealed that “I was like, ‘Why not?’” she recalls thinking. “I had a kid and put my life on hold for a little bit. I wanted to do something more. I was like, ‘This body is not done.’ [I] went to a tryout, had no experience at all.”.

In a recent development, jade left that tryout bruised and battered—and determined to improve. And so she trained and trained and trained some more. She couldn’t get enough. “I just loved it,” she says. “It's athletics, yes, but also it's improvising, but also it's acting, but also it's your natural instinct. It’s all these things wrapped into one that I just didn't want to put down.”.

All that work eventually paid off: Jade made her professional wrestling debut with All Elite Wrestling in 2020 and then joined the WWE three years later.

Despite all the training and preparation that goes into a match, Jade admits that not a single one has been “perfect.” But in the case where she stumbles off the ropes or throws a lousy punch, Jade simply follows the old maxim, the show must go on.

According to recent reports, “I just kind of have the mindset that these things happen,” she notes. “If you do have a mishap, you can't sell it—[the audience doesn’t] know what's going on. You just got to keep going with the punches.”.

Jade also gives a lot of credit to her fellow competitors, who often pick her up—if not physically, then emotionally—after a match, letting her know she’s not alone.

“I remember my coworker Naomi sent me a clip of her falling, and she was like, ‘Just to show you...’ And I was like, ‘Okay, all right. It happens,’” Jade claims. “You’ve just got to keep on going and make your next match the best match.”.

Sources indicate that as a mom, Jade knows how powerful an adult’s example can be—whether it’s a parent’s or a performer’s. Ultimately, she hopes kids are inspired by her hard work and determination, both in and out of the ring, and if they can take away any message, it would be this: “Don't let anyone tell you who you are,” she says. “Don't let society put you in a box. Go out there and take on the world.”.

Sources indicate that and when a new opportunity presents itself, don’t be afraid to give it a try. “If you would have told me five years ago, I would be wrestling. I would have laughed,” she says. “And look at me now.”.

To hear more from Jade—including her no-frills recovery program—click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above.

Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

📅 24 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.
  • The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.
  • Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

Sources indicate that “Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”.

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”.

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Industry observers note that participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova remarked. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”.

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

Recent findings suggest that “This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That stated, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”.

It has been revealed that sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:.

It has been revealed that “Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”.

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she mentioned. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”.

According to recent reports, prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” noted that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”.

Tech Report: Iceland’s first wind farm comes with a water-saving bonus

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.
  • According to recent reports, vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads.
  • Sources indicate that landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power company, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.

According to recent reports, vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads. And Iceland’s windiest months coincide with the time of year when less water flows into its reservoirs.

Sources indicate that landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power company, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026. The first 14 turbines are online; another 14 will be installed in a second phase, and the entire wind farm is expected to be operating by the end of 2027.

Once complete, Vaðölduver will have 120 megawatts (MW) of capacity. When I met with the folks at Landsvirkjun in Reykjavik last month, they told me that’s enough to power the equivalent of 90,000 Icelandic households. Vaðalda’s electricity feeds into the grid and is sold through power purchase agreements.

Vaðölduver sits on a lava-and-sand plain east of the Þjórsá River, south of Sultartangi Dam. Landsvirkjun already operates seven hydropower stations in the surrounding Þjórsá and Tungnaá region.

The wind farm was sited in this region of Iceland because the seasons line up nicely.

Industry observers note that the winds are strongest in winter, when inflows into hydropower reservoirs can be low. In summer, wind speeds tend to drop, but glacial melt increases water availability for the hydropower system.

According to recent reports, when the wind turbines are generating plenty of electricity, Landsvirkjun can ease off hydropower and leave more water in its reservoirs. When the wind drops, hydropower can pick up more of the demand.

That gives the utility more control over when it uses its stored water and helps that water go further.

Industry observers note that german wind turbine maker Enercon manufactured Vaðölduver’s turbines. The project also includes a service and maintenance agreement with Enercon.

Landsvirkjun had a decade of experience operating pilot wind turbines before building Vaðölduver. One substantial thing they learned: They didn’t need tall towers to find plenty of wind.

There’s little vegetation or other surface obstructions across this unique, exposed landscape. That allows the turbines to capture productive winds closer to the ground than they could at a more wooded or sheltered location.

Recent findings suggest that “Lower” is relative, of course. The turbines still reach 150 meters (492 feet) at their highest blade tip.

In a recent development, the wind farm covers 17.1 square kilometers (6.6 square miles). Twenty-five turbines are rated at 4.26 MW each, and the remaining three at 4.5 MW. Landsvirkjun’s presentation puts annual generation at 440 GWh and lists a P50 net efficiency figure of 43%, which is considered strong for onshore wind.

The ability to tap into existing infrastructure was a major factor in Landsvirkjun’s site selection. Where a wind farm goes affects its cost, its environmental footprint, and the people who live nearby.

Landsvirkjun also identifies active engagement with communities and other stakeholders as essential to building wind projects. At Vaðölduver, the immediate task is to finish the remaining 14 turbines while the first phase completes its trial runs.

The manufacturer sees wind as a potential third pillar of Iceland’s electricity supply alongside hydropower and geothermal. Vaðölduver reveals how those resources can work together, with wind adding generation while helping conserve stored water.

Recent findings suggest that iceland is a world leader in clean energy. It generates nearly 100% of its electricity from renewable sources, combining hydropower fueled by glacial runoff and rivers (around 70%) and geothermal energy (around 30%).

Over 90% of Icelandic households use direct geothermal hot water for space heating and hot water, while the remaining homes use renewable electricity.

But it’s got the same grid capacity challenges as every other country. Adding wind – and anything else that uses power – means paying close attention to what the grid can handle. Iceland has an isolated transmission system, so maintaining stability and ensuring sufficient capacity are increasingly important as the country develops more projects.

According to recent reports, while in Reykjavik, I met with the Minister of the Environment, Energy and Climate, Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson, who told me that the Icelandic grid’s capacity is expected to grow from 20 TWh to 24-25 TWh within a decade. Jóhannsson also stated that he is pro-data center and that investors are keen to establish more of them in the country.

Recent findings suggest that when I asked Jóhannsson and his team, as well as the teams at Landsvirkjun and publicly owned ON Power, Iceland’s second-largest electricity generator and largest EV charger network, about grid expansion aims to handle that pipeline, they all remarked that legislative reforms were being passed to speed up energy permitting processes. There is also financing in place to grow the grid. The physical transmission network is being expanded, but the process is slow because NIMBYism is creating bottlenecks.

In learning about newly introduced and completed Icelandic power projects during my visit, it was apparent that the companies in the power and geothermal heat sector regularly collaborate on projects – everyone brings their expertise to the table and works for the common good (yes, really).

Sources indicate that but what was striking in discussions about grid expansion was that there seemed to be no looks to pitch in with the Icelandic transmission system operator (TSO), Landsnet hf. It seemed that the strategy was to let the TSO come up with the solutions on its own. At most, Jóhannsson’s team remarked its legislative reform “opened the door” to possible grid innovations.

When I asked the Landsvirkjun team whether they were considering working with the TSO on distributed energy resource (DER) projects like virtual power plants and onsite battery storage for its heavy-industry clients, which make up 80% of its business, they said they hadn’t considered it.

I often wonder why Quebec hasn't followed this strategy. They have huge dams with world-leading power connections, and one of the problem they are facing is a lack of water to refill those dams, due to several years of relative drought. I know it costs a lot to build wind power up north, but siting a project there would re-use their massive investment in power lines. The dams would act as gigantic batteries, because they wouldn't need to drain their reservoirs when the wind is blowing.

Iceland has earned its reputation as a clean energy leader. Bringing that same collaborative and creative approach to expanding its grid would help it keep setting an example for the rest of the world.

TESTING HIKING BOOTS, trail shoes, camping gear, and the like for a living means I spend a lot of time outdoors. Living in the Edwin B. Forsythe National Wildlife Refuge in coastal New Jersey, I’m fortunate to be able to step out my door and immediately be right in the middle of nature.

Recent findings suggest that and when the weather starts to get colder, I take that as a cue not to head indoors, but to layer up. That means the hooded wetsuit goes on, an assortment of puffer jackets get put through the paces, and base layers become the first line of defense. With the holiday season upon us, here are six gifts that fellow nature lovers will find useful in the coming year. Better yet—they’re all available for purchase at Tractor Supply Co.

While Yeti’s coolers are certainly premium investments, the brand’s drinkware comprises some of its most accessible, hard-wearing products. Yes, the Yeti Rambler Water Bottle has been our best water bottle since it was released, but an insulated version is a must for anyone looking to stay outdoors. This 20-ounce stackable one is great because you can keep a few stacked in your camp kitchen gear and always know you’ve got mugs for the campsite.

In a recent development, the Carhartt knit beanie has experienced a resurgence in popularity over the past couple winters, and for good reason: It’s affordable, it’s comfy in an acrylic knit, it comes in a ton of great colors, and it’s gonna last for years. While you really can’t go wrong with any color, I’m pretty partial to the traditional Carhartt brown, which evokes the iconic canvas Duck Jacket.

Recent findings suggest that my hands get pretty thrashed throughout the year surfing in the cold and constantly being outside, and the harsh, dry winter air is not very kind to them. I do my best with wearing gloves in the cold, but when I’m shooting photos of wildlife or practicing other hobbies that call for maximum dexterity, I sometimes fall short. That means I eventually get some cracked knuckles and need a repair balm like this aptly named option from Duke Cannon. It’s made with lanolin, which means it doesn’t leave my hands sticky or greasy like other lotions and balms tend to do.

Industry observers note that speaking of gloves, if I’m outside and not being super active (say, just walking the dog), or need to protect my hands while doing yardwork or bringing firewood into the house for the wood-burning stove, I turn to a leather pair like these. They tend to wear in, not out. And you can always just sport some cheapy knit gloves underneath if you want more insulation. Hearty gloves like this are always a must-have for campsite duty.

It has been revealed that the nature preserve I live in is part of a pretty active salt-marsh tidal zone, and a creek runs behind my house that I launch my canoe and paddleboard from. This way of life requires me to be cognizant of (and really in tune with) the tides. It also requires a good pair of muck boots, because some days even just walking the dog means trekking through water. Deck boots (or those shorter ones that go just above the ankle) are pretty pointless in this sort of area—you really want something taller like these knee-highs, which are insulated and keep you dry all day long.

It has been revealed that A thin (read: not puffy) vest is an overlooked layering option for the outdoors. It can function as an outer layer on warmer days, and when it cools off it still fits seamlessly under a shell or puffer. This reversible Field & Stream option is a solid choice because it’s water-resistant on one side and has soft polyester fleece on the other (adding even more insulation). And that cuffed neck is great for full coverage when it gets chilly.

He has written about the outdoors for nearly two decades and was previously the Managing Editor, Content Performance at Gear Patrol. Ryan currently lives on the water in Upcoming Jersey with his wife and their dog.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the rarest and most coveted coins in United States history is headed for the auction block this week, where it could sell for over $2 million. But while collectors have long dreamed about owning one of the five existing 1885 silver trade dollars, the strange story of their creation remains murky more than 140 years after their minting.

The U.S. struck the first trade dollars in 1873 as a way to compete with similar silver coinage in East Asia, but the production was short-lived. Silver market fluctuations and foreign policy shifts led to their demonetization in 1876, and they were only minted for collectors beginning in 1879. By 1884, the U.S. commissioned only 10 trade dollars before finally retiring the series destroying the die casts.

However, a thoroughly corrupt political appointee named A. Loudon Snowden had other looks. Snowden’s career in currencies began in 1857, when his uncle and former Treasurer of Pennsylvania hired the then 22-year-old whippersnapper at the Philadelphia Mint. While at the mint, he pursued various personal profiteering interests, including the clandestine production and selling of thousands of rare coins for collectors.In 1885, Snowden finally retired as Superintendent of the Philadelphia Mint after nearly three decades.

Industry observers note that snowden also gave himself a parting gift before retiring—five 1885 trade dollars that he purchased from the Mint cashier. No one knew of their existence until a year after Snowden’s death in 1912. The first 1885 trade dollar auctioned in 1913 for $1,140 (about $32,174 in current valuation).

Although some numismatists and historians argue Snowden’s five trade dollars were a final grift, other experts argue that the coins have a surprisingly mundane backstory. Until the 1930’s, Mint employees were legally allowed to purchase examples of newly introduced coinage for their equivalent amount. Snowden did just this when he previously bought 10 proof 1884 trade dollars, and it’s possible he bought the following year’s coins before the decision not to mint any others. Regardless of the true story, only five 1885 trade dollars exist today—and they’re worth far more than Snowden could ever imagine.

Stack’s Bowers will auction the 1885 trade dollar as part of its Rarities Night series on Tuesday, November 17.

Update 11/18/2026 12:50 p.m. EST: Stack’s Bowers confirmed its 1885 trade dollar sold for just over $1.95 million.

Why So Many Upcoming Moms Are Told to Wait to Exercise Again—and What the Research Really Notes

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment.
  • Sources indicate that “I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter claims.
  • The problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment. Her point wasn’t that fresh moms should rush back to the gym. It was that one timeline can’t fit everyone. Some women are ready to move sooner, and others need more time.

The Reel ruffled some feathers.

Sources indicate that “I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter claims. “But that's definitely not what we're saying.” (By “we,” she means trainers who keep up with the latest research on pregnancy and postpartum exercise.).

The problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence. On the contrary, research suggests that this type of blanket advice doesn’t make sense for something as personal as postpartum recovery. When you return to exercise after childbirth should depend on your own symptoms, not a date on the calendar.

“There's really nothing magical about the six-week time point,” indicates Margie Davenport, PhD, a professor of kinesiology at the University of Alberta and chair of the 2025 Canadian Guidelines for Physical Activity for Pregnancy and Postpartum—the first-ever exercise guidelines to specifically focus on evidence-based suggestions for that first year postpartum. In the U.S., the main guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) covers pregnancy and the postpartum period together. ACOG’s guidance points in the same direction, though: It says many women can start exercising again within days of an uncomplicated birth. In fact, “there is no identified ideal time to return,” Davenport says.

In a recent development, based on the wide range of comments on Carpenter’s post—some supportive, some hypercritical, and still others asking more questions to try to better understand this shift away from the advice they’ve always heard—there’s still a lot of confusion around postpartum exercise. So we asked experts to break down what the research actually states, and how to approach working out in this fresh chapter of life.

In a recent development, in many cultures, the first 30 or 40 days postpartum is traditionally considered a protected time to rest, relax, and recover, Davenport states. In Chinese culture, it’s called zuo yuezi, which translates to “sitting the month.” In many Latin American and Latino communities, it’s known as “la cuarentena,” a nod to its roughly 40-day length. In South Korea, it’s sanhujori, or “postpartum care.”.

In a recent development, these traditions carry deep cultural significance and are meant to offer real healing and support after birth from one’s community (they put “it takes a village” into practice). They’re rooted in caregiving and cultural custom, and they were never meant to serve as a medical timeline for when it’s safe to start exercising.

It has been revealed that in Western medicine, six weeks has become an key medical benchmark in postpartum recovery—and, over time, a default point for returning to exercise too. “At that point, your uterus should be back to its pre-pregnancy state, and so a lot of the gynecologic changes should be fairly reversed by that point,” indicates Rita Deering, DPT, PhD, associate professor of exercise science and director of the Pelvic Health, Exercise & Musculoskeletal (PHEM) Research Laboratory at Marquette University.

In a recent development, the first six weeks after birth are also when the risk of complications like high blood pressure and infection is highest, Deering says, which is part of why that window became an important medical checkpoint (even though some pregnancy-related changes take longer to resolve). But, she says, “it was never intended to be about exercise.”.

Recent findings suggest that so how did six weeks become the exercise rule? Before researchers knew much about how safe it is to exercise during pregnancy and after birth, working out was considered potentially risky, Deering notes. There wasn’t strong evidence that exercise wouldn’t slow healing or raise the odds of complications. So the most cautious advice was simply to wait until a doctor confirmed you’d healed enough to resume physical activity.

It has been revealed that to come up with the 2025 Canadian Guidelines, researchers did a deep dive of all the available research on the topic, which included 574 unique studies organized into seven systematic reviews based on 21 different outcomes of postpartum exercise—such as depression and anxiety, low-back pain, injuries, glucose and blood pressure levels, and more. They also assembled an international panel of experts to give their recommendations.

Industry observers note that their advice: Start light-intensity physical activity and mobilization (think: carrying your baby around your home, a slow walk down the block, pelvic floor physical therapy) right away. From there, progress as you feel ready to moderate-to-vigorous activity such as brisk walking, resistance training, and running at your own pace—as long as tears and incisions have sufficiently healed and you don’t experience additional bleeding with exercise. (As mentioned, ACOG similarly recommends that women can return to postnatal exercise within days after an uncomplicated birth.).

Recent findings suggest that based on the research, there are no “absolute contraindications” to exercise postpartum, Davenport says—meaning no condition would rule out exercise entirely. There are some relative contraindications, she explains, “where you might have to delay a little bit or modify the type of activity that you're doing.” Examples include severe abdominal pain, extreme fatigue, and C-section incision pain that worsens with activity. All warrant a conversation with your doctor before starting.

Want to Know More About Lifting While Pregnant? Start Here.

Recent findings suggest that pelvic floor symptoms, like leaking urine or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina, aren’t a reason to stop exercising altogether. If you notice signs of pelvic floor dysfunction, the guidelines recommend starting slowly and building up gradually instead. “Some leakage is okay,” Davenport states. “It means that the training that you’re doing is just overloading the muscle.”.

Many people, including plenty of commenters on Carpenter’s Reel, worry that exercising after birth will damage the pelvic floor and cause dysfunction. But the evidence doesn’t support that. In fact, those muscles will likely be better off if you resume training, especially if you do exercises to target them in particular. “Engaging in pelvic floor muscle training reduces your risk of urinary incontinence by around 37 percent,” Davenport claims. Additionally, if you stop all exercise because you're leaking a little bit, “this can actually mean that you're missing out on those other benefits.”.

One caveat: If you’re leaking a lot, or it’s getting worse over time, “you probably need to pull it back,” Davenport states. That means being more selective about the moves you choose. For example, you might skip long runs and high-impact moves like jump squats for now, adds Sheridan Skye, a registered nurse, pre- and postnatal fitness coach, and founder of The Female Fitness Formula. Stick with lower-impact exercises, then build up gradually as you get stronger and your symptoms level off or improve.

It has been revealed that at the end of the day, every body, birth, and recovery is vastly different. “Some people have a very uncomplicated labor and delivery and pregnancy; for others, it's quite complex,” notes Davenport. “It only makes sense that the way that they're returning and what time they're actually returning is also going to be quite individualized.”.

For some new moms, six weeks is too soon, and a blanket deadline only adds stress. “Maybe they aren't sleeping or they don't have the support to be able to return [to exercise] at six weeks,” Davenport notes. On the flip side, for someone who had a straightforward delivery and is itching to get moving again, “telling them to wait for six weeks with no evidence to support it is also inappropriate.”.

Sources indicate that in fact, exercise can offer significant benefits during postpartum recovery, even before the six-week mark. “It improves muscle and bone density that we lose throughout pregnancy,” Skye notes. Postpartum exercise is associated with a 45 percent reduction in the odds of developing postpartum depression, and starting before 12 weeks is even more beneficial.

It’s also associated with a 28 percent reduction in the risk of developing diabetes postpartum. Exercise even improves sleep quality, Skye notes. “Women tend to feel more energized and like they've experienced more rest, even if they haven't,” she says. (Anyone who’s survived a 3 a.m. feeding stretch knows that’s no small thing!).

There is also evidence that exercise in general can help to decrease pain, says Deering, and research links sedentary behavior to lumbopelvic (the areas of the lower back and pelvis) pain. “So if you are having pain, movement might be what you need to help with that.”.

For many people, it may be difficult to know if you’re truly ready. “Especially when you're postpartum, it can feel like you are super out of touch with your body sensations, especially if you're not sleeping well,” Carpenter says.

It has been revealed that if you're at the point where you're thinking about it, but are nervous or unsure or just overwhelmed by having another decision to make, Davenport recommends taking the Get Active Questionnaire for Postpartum—a tool that her team designed as part of the 2025 guideline. It can help you rapidly understand if you’re ready to start from a medical perspective. That can help give you some reassurance.

Recent findings suggest that there can also be “a lot of fear involved,” Carpenter indicates, especially if you had a C-section or are healing from a vaginal tear. In that case, “you’re probably going to be a bit hesitant,” which is completely understandable. Starting slower and lighter than you think you need to is perfectly fine as you get reacquainted with your body. “The first several sessions are really about mentally trying to get that confidence back,” she says.

As you go, pay attention to how your body responds. Leaking, for instance? That’s not a reason to stop exercising, but you may want to adjust your workout to reduce it. More bleeding, new pain, or a sense that something just doesn’t feel right are signs to stop, reassess, and possibly scale back. If they don’t improve, check in with your doctor. “It’s really about setting your ego aside and being willing to modify, even if it’s one rep to the next, based on how you’re feeling right at that time,” Carpenter states.

In a recent development, and if you feel physically ready but aren’t quite there mentally? “It’s okay to honor those feelings,” Deering says, “and to recognize that it’s okay to give yourself some time.” Whether that’s two weeks, six weeks, or six months, the right moment to start moving is the one that works for you.

Amy is a freelance writer and editor who covers health, fitness, and lifestyle topics—with a focus on practical advice that fits into real life. She previously worked as deputy fitness editor at SELF, and is both an ACE-certified personal trainer and a ProNatal pre and postnatal fitness specialist. Her work has been published in Women’s Health, Men’s Health, SELF, Wondermind, HGTV, Outside, REAL SIMPLE, The New York Times for Kids, and more. Amy lives in central New York where she spends her off-hours chasing after her two kids, digging into backyard gardening projects with her husband, and creatively squeezing at-home workouts into her schedule as often as she can.

#110608. Industry News: Are AI Design Visualizers Selling Us on Slop?

Industry News: Are AI Design Visualizers Selling Us on Slop?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Can I interest you in an autonomous sauna rideshare?
  • These objects—or slopjects, as their creator calls them—are not real.
  • The slopject’s unsavory first cousin, the slopspace—a full-scale interior scheme, created through digital rendering, and now generative AI—is increasingly populating home-decor inspiration sites like this one, where a viewer can encounter improbable living scenarios like garage apartments with no ladders or stairs to reach the lofted bed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Can I interest you in an autonomous sauna rideshare? How about a conversation pit car? Or a Magic 8 Ball in the shape of Rick Rubin? How about a plate for a single almond or a toilet turntable?

Friends, do I even need to say it? These objects—or slopjects, as their creator calls them—are not real. Though they look convincing on the feed, they don’t exist in meatspace the way that you or I do. They are Dadaist fantasies, dreamed up and rendered digitally without the limitations of production budgets, market demand, or even those pesky things known as laws.

The slopject’s unsavory first cousin, the slopspace—a full-scale interior scheme, created through digital rendering, and now generative AI—is increasingly populating home-decor inspiration sites like this one, where a viewer can encounter improbable living scenarios like garage apartments with no ladders or stairs to reach the lofted bed.

It has been revealed that with hyperrealistic renderings a mere prompt away (and disclosures of AI-generated content remaining spotty at best), it’s getting harder to tell what’s real. On platforms like Pinterest and Instagram, where homeowners often seek inspiration for their design projects, the speculative images that float through the digital ether can be particularly hard to detect. Entire subreddits are dedicated to sniffing them out.

And detection is just the beginning. Aside from struggling to detangle fact from fiction in stumbled-upon images, consumers are also using LLMs—or large language models, AI tools designed to work with human speech—to generate their own visions of their dream home, without always understanding what it takes to make those fantasies a reality. That dynamic is starting to have concrete consequences for the professionals charged with designing and building the rooms we live in, where dollars and cents, artisanal skill, and the laws of physics remain painfully real. (Just ask the guy who tried to exit the lofted bed without a ladder.).

“People are seeing or prompting more fantastical solutions that are not rooted in the reality of the built environment, and then they’re presenting those to us as something that can be executed,” indicates Kevin Greenberg, founder and principal of the AD PRO Directory–listed firm Space Exploration Design. “We do it diplomatically and we do it politely, but we will tell them, ‘Oh, you know, it’s really difficult to achieve a stone ceiling.’”.

This change is happening fast. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index Report notes that more than half of the population has started using generative AI in the past three years—a swiftness that outpaces both personal computers and the internet itself. When Midjourney and other AI imaging tools first hit the market, Greenberg notes, clients used them to test the limits of what was aesthetically possible. “The prompt was like, ‘tropical Tudor fantasy,’ and then we were left to clean up the mess,” he recalls. “The images we were seeing were just tacky, and we all got a really big belly laugh out of it.” No one’s laughing now, he says.

These days, homeowners are feeding designer-created collages, mood boards, and sketches into Claude to see what spaces might look like once they’re built. The results tend to be uncanny: surfaces gleam like the Las Vegas strip, proportions are wonky, and there’s an unsettling feeling of dead air. Cy and Genevieve Carter, the principals of the New York City–based interiors firm Carter Design, joke that the worst dig they can make on a space is to say it feels like standing inside of a rendering. In the world of AI images, “there’s not a simplicity of space,” claims Genevieve, which often means that more subtle textures like plaster don’t properly register.

Recent findings suggest that jake Shapiro, the owner of Hudson Valley–based millwork studio Slabrock, compares the images produced through AI software to the bloodless cuisine now rendered on deli signs. “It looks like scrambled eggs, but it also looks like H.P. Lovecraft, and that’s just horrific,” he says. “The same thing exists in design.”.

There’s treachery in these images, designers agree, in that they portray a space nearly—but not quite—photorealistically. While that theoretically might help a homeowner understand how a designer’s vision for a space maps onto the real thing, it also bakes in a false sense of exactness that can leave room for misunderstanding or even disappointment. Organic materials like wood, for instance, can be difficult to predict with precision in AI. Every tree is different, Shapiro points out.

Recent findings suggest that catherine Campbell Pearson, a set designer and stylist based in Brooklyn, is seeing AI-fantasy expectations infiltrate the environments she designs for photoshoots too. In the past she and her clients would work from a “comp,” or a Photoshopped portrayal of the imagined end shoot. With those more lo-fi pictures, there was an understanding that the finished product would look slightly different. That’s disappearing in the age of GenAI: “It’s such a cohesive version of their idea that there’s much more attachment to the finished product looking exactly like this AI image.”.

This phenomenon has real consequences for designers, whose expertise is on the line when a rendering goes awry. When clients go off on their own and submit designers’ early proposals into AI platforms, “The rendering that it produces is really unsexy and clunky and ugly,” notes Greenberg. “Then they’re looking at us like, ‘Well, you’re actually not that good at your job.’”.

What these examples illustrate isn’t a fresh problem, exactly, but it is one that’s more apparent in the age of AI. Just as Pearson has relied on low-resolution comps to create environments in the past, designers often use tools like collage, drawings, and mood boards to gesture at vibe and design intent before progressing to a more dialed-in rendering. But most homeowners don’t have the language to communicate exactly what they want to a designer—and when they do, the language may not precisely match the listener’s interpretation. (One person’s “cozy” interior is another’s clutter-filled nightmare, just as one person’s “serene” oasis is another’s sterile dystopia.).

LLMs offer clients a way to articulate their ideas in a way they may not have been able to otherwise—but in doing so, they create a highly specific rendering for a space that will require negotiation with real materials, labor, and budget—the latter being a serious constraint where AI can cause problems, claims Tyler Polich, cofounder of the Los Angeles–based firm Years Studio. He shares an example of a client fiddling with an image and generating an element fully clad in copper—an option he and his partner would have never presented because of the cost. “Maybe it makes for a compelling image,” he concedes, “but we know that Gemini just blew their budget immediately.”.

Industry observers note that in certain cases, these visualizations can simplify things for designers and clients. Lucca Zeray, the Berkshires-based maker of Lucca House modular shelving, has found the addition of an AI rendering tool—a “configurator” that can depict his brand’s color-edged units in the proportions they’re seeking and provide a cost estimate—to be a game changer in the ordering process. “It’s a way that we can be like, ‘Here, you draw it,’ and close the gap,” he says. Unlike the every-detail-on-the-table possibilities of a full interior design rendering, Zeray’s configurator is only manipulating a few straightforward options, which might be part of the reason for its success.

In the reality of a built design, image making is only a small piece of the puzzle. The real work is in executing—navigating the personal relationships, sourcing fabricators, and negotiating details with the give and take of material reality. “We don’t work just in ideas,” claims Genevieve Carter. “We work in stuff and things, and people, and their expertise is still a dialogue.”.

Beyond the making itself, the design still needs to be good. Before AI was widely adopted, the algorithm-fueled flattening of taste was already in the cultural crosshairs. Social platforms reward likeable, heavily publicized images, like Athena Calderone’s marble-wrapped Brooklyn kitchen—photos that have been shared again and again. The problem then becomes that everyone is asking for an Athena Calederone–style kitchen. (It’s worth noting that even Calderone herself seems to have moved on from this look, by the way—her most recent home tour features a much moodier, Art Deco–inflected interior.) In today’s technological climate, this dilemma is taking a new form, as visuals take shape based on all of the environments that have been photographed and put online. But, claims Polich, there’s an inherent flaw in this system: “The vast amount of visual information is relatively mediocre.” Real estate websites, DIY blogs, e-commerce images—most of the internet doesn’t look like, well, AD. It’s designed to be crowd-pleasing and just fine, not necessarily something extraordinary or innovative.

According to recent reports, years Studio similarly seeks to tease out its clients’ personalities—“something that is real and human and only exists in them,” as Polich puts it. That’s a vulnerable undertaking, but also one that AI cannot replicate when its foundation is built on remixing what’s already come before. Greenberg, the Carters, and Polich all recognize that there’s some element of a trust fall required on the client’s side. By the end of a project, a designer is often familiar with the most intimate details of their client’s life—even what they keep in their nightstand. (They see those specialty chargers, and they don’t judge.).

But in earning trust, ironically, AI is also occasionally lending designers an assist. For the Carters, an exacting client was reassured in the studio’s recommendation of a particular stone after she’d exhausted all of the other options herself in her AI engine of choice. Another time, they won over a prospect by tweaking his AI rendering, and suggesting color options the client hadn’t considered. Is it possible that Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini could remind homeowners why they hired a designer in the first place? Just ask the Rick Rubin Magic 8 ball: Signs point to yes.

Old solar panels have silver and copper worth recovering. A new US recycling tech giant called Jupiter looks to send metals recovered from retired solar panels and data center hardware to Korea Zinc’s refineries, including a $7.4 billion plant planned for Clarksville, Tennessee.

Jupiter joins US solar panel recycler Solarcycle and PedalPoint Recycling, Korea Zinc’s US recycling and metals business, into a single, fully integrated manufacturer. Jupiter says it’s launching with eight certified US facilities, nearly 1 million square feet of processing space, and about 250 employees. It’s also taking on customers from both businesses, including Microsoft, Prologis, and Brookfield.

It has been revealed that for a solar farm or data center operator, that means a single tech giant can take equipment out of service, resell parts with remaining useful life, and recycle the rest. Customers can track where the materials go and bring them back into their own supply chains.

Industry observers note that korea Zinc will hold a majority stake. Solarcycle’s Suvi Sharma will lead Jupiter as CEO, and PedalPoint’s Kevin Hahm will be CFO. Microsoft and Prologis Ventures are among Solarcycle’s existing investors.

As Electrek reported in January, Solarcycle’s Cedartown, Georgia, plant was processing thousands of old solar panels a week when it opened. Solarcycle stated the plant could handle up to 5 gigawatts’ worth of panels annually at full capacity, recovering materials such as glass, aluminum, copper, and silver.

According to recent reports, the Tennessee plant adds a US refining step. Korea Zinc is developing the facility, called Project Crucible, with US government backing. It expects to start production in phases in 2029. The plant is designed to process about 1.1 million tons of raw materials per year and produce roughly 540,000 tons of finished products.

Shadow welcomes unknown female bald eagle to his nest

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Internet-famous bald eagle Shadow has endured an up-and-down 2026.
  • After the August death of Jackie, the female eagle he raised chicks with since 2018, Shadow began spending time with a 4-year-old female eagle named Kaydee (formerly KD1).
  • Cameras spotted the unknown female in the nest in recent weeks, but this was the first time the eagle was joined by Shadow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Internet-famous bald eagle Shadow has endured an up-and-down 2026. From suffering the loss of a clutch of eggs to welcoming two chicks, and from losing his longtime partner to finding a fresh friend, he’s had a tumultuous year.

After the August death of Jackie, the female eagle he raised chicks with since 2018, Shadow began spending time with a 4-year-old female eagle named Kaydee (formerly KD1). Viewers of the 24/7 livestream of Shadow’s nest could easily spot Kaydee because of her double-banded legs—a silver ring on one leg and a lavender one on the other. The pair appeared chummy as they spent more time together, sharing stick-arranging duties, singing, and exchanging beaky kisses. An unexpected twist arrived this week with the appearance of an unknown female bald eagle spotted in the nest with Shadow.

Cameras spotted the unknown female in the nest in recent weeks, but this was the first time the eagle was joined by Shadow. On Monday afternoon, Shadow landed in the nest quickly followed by the unknown female. The unknown female fiddled the nest sticks while vocalizing and Shadow appeared unbothered by her presence. Eagles will typically defend their nest from intruders so Shadow’s willingness to share his space with an eagle other than Kaydee surprised many viewers.

Shadow returned the nest solo later in the afternoon as the sun set over Substantial Bear Lake.

Industry observers note that as this is nature, all we can do is sit back and see what unfolds. Mating season is approaching, so we have to wait and see if Shadow selects a new partner. Female eagles in Significant Bear Valley typically lay their first clutch of eggs in January. Tune in to Friends of Big Bear Valley’s (FOBBV) livestreams to follow the southern California eagles anytime.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

Kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee at the moment has a black spot on her head, but it may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate. She was recently spotted on FOBBV’s livestream inspecting the nest and has also been seen hanging out near Shadow. Flying around Substantial Bear is completely normal behavior for young adult eagles at this time of year.

Recent findings suggest that in January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

In a recent development, she was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below six percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

According to recent reports, A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Big Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.
