💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in New York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein.
  • Pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint.
  • Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in New York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein. Pawson, then an architectural wunderkind from the United Kingdom, and Smith-Petersen, a young Danish-Italian communications manager for the fashion house, found themselves collaborating on the opening of the brand’s first flagship on Madison Avenue.

Pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint. His earliest residential works (a Mallorca summer house for collectors, an art dealer’s London apartment) provided a series of simple surfaces, plinths, and frames—for objects, for vistas, and for life. The same was true at the Calvin Klein store, where designer and client amplified each other’s design approaches in a meeting of minimalist minds.

Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.

The living area features a table and chairs by Poul Kjærholm.

A sauna is clad in blackened wood.

Pawson’s recent residence for Smith-Petersen and her husband, Enrico Erba Springorum, an Armani executive, makes another case for life with less. “The imprint came from childhood: the minimalism, the Danish design,” explains Smith-Petersen, who grew up outside Copenhagen. “Poul Kjærholm was our neighbor,” she adds, name-checking the widely influential midcentury modernist. There were also formative summers spent at the pared-back house her father designed on the Turkish peninsula of Çeşme. About the location, she recalls, “People stated, ‘You guys are crazy!’ But it was a place close to nature and the sea. And then later it became a destination.”.

A single sculptural tree dots the courtyard.

An oak bed with integrated bedside tables anchors the primary bedroom.

Ninety minutes south of Milan, the patchwork hills of the Val Luretta are far less isolated. Its proximity to the city has attracted editors, artists, and other creatives in search of space and quiet. That tranquility drew Smith-Petersen to the area when she was seeking land on which to build a compound with her younger brother, Henrik, for their families. (She and her husband have two adult sons.) Over the years, she and Pawson had maintained a friendship. “So when Henrik and I found the property, I had this crazy idea: Why don’t I ask John?” says Smith-Petersen. “My brother mentioned, ‘Forget it!’ But we went to visit John and his team in London and it kicked off from there.”.

The primary bath’s bespoke vanity, topped in a Grassi Pietri surface.

Smith-Petersen stands in the living area.

A view across the dining table toward the minimalist hearth.

The resulting structure, realized with project architect Giulio Marchesi, is the irst of two planned homes on the site, one for each sibling. Sitting long and low on the land, like an ivory piano key dropped onto the hillside, the single-story house frames expansive views of the Val Luretta. “The area of the countryside is so dramatic,” reflects Pawson, whose first visit to the site was in winter fog. “In the summer, it’s very different—it’s so lush.”.

It has been revealed that at some 2,500 square feet, the house is spacious but intimate, with Pawson’s trademark spareness and remarkable warmth. He designed it along one axis, a long corridor connecting the foyer to the open-plan kitchen, dining area, and living area, then bedrooms beyond. White-painted plaster walls and floors of pale-gray stone, sourced nearby in Vicenza, radiate calm. As Pawson explains, understanding the way the body and the eye move through a space is paramount—and can take time. “You’ve got to learn the choreography,” he states. Living in and feeling the house is key.

Smith-Petersen and Pawson on-site.

Industry observers note that the yearslong friendship Pawson and Smith-Petersen had forged helped him understand how she would use the space. There would be mornings at the Pawson-designed table, afternoons on the terrace or under one of the century-old oaks, and evenings making dinner in a kitchen brimming with Scandinavian tableware. In solitude or surrounded by family, there’s complete peace on offer.

The open-plan dining area and kitchen.

Sources indicate that “Most architects—contemporaries, colleagues—always say, ‘Oh, it’s impossible, a private house,’ ” says Pawson. The process can be “very emotional. And that’s what makes it good.” Luckily for Smith-Petersen, the primary feeling the house evokes is serenity. “I didn’t expect to be in such awe,” she says. “I was never a country person. Sometimes, I try to arrive a day before anyone else is here and do a silent retreat,” she adds. “It’s where I feel best now. It’s pure joy.”.

"What Does This Mean For Me?" When Life Is All About Ourself

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that we don't interact with our life directly; we interact with what life means about us.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

It has been revealed that this is part 2 in a series. You can read part 1 here.

Sources indicate that we don't interact with our life directly; we interact with what life means about us. What if the problem isn't that life isn't meeting our needs? What if the problem is that getting our personal needs met has become the single focus of our life?

According to recent reports, in part 1 of this series, I discussed the many ways we’re conditioned and wired to be self-focused in today’s world, to constantly monitor and manage our own okay-ness and whether our needs are being met. And furthermore, how each moment is experienced as what we've decided it says about us. Does this situation, conversation, decision, opinion make me feel less than or better than? Does it make me feel valued, comfortable, seen? Does it validate my story of “who I am”? I posited the idea that viewing our lives through the lens of “does this serve me?” is, at its root, an attempt to be happy, shore ourselves up, and ultimately, survive. While, in fact, we’ve got it wrong: putting “me” at the center of the universe and the reason everything happens ends up making us suffer.

So what exactly is the suffering that comes with our relentless self-focus—what’s wrong with seeing everything through the lens of how it affects “me”?

Recent findings suggest that when we experience every situation and everyone else's choices through the lens of “self,” as fundamentally a commentary on how we're doing and a referendum on our worth, then every moment carries the potential to wound, undermine, humiliate, and destroy us. Every interaction can threaten who we think we are. We have to remain hyper-vigilant, therefore, on high alert for whether we’re okay or not okay, and any experience that feels like it doesn’t support our story of ourselves, which can also include a simple difference of opinion.

We live in a constant state of “not-enoughness.” We can never get enough approval, recognition, validation, reassurance, success, or reflection. The self that needs to be continually affirmed is never permanently satisfied; whatever we “get” only lasts as long as this particular experience. We imagine that if we win this argument or get this situation to “go our way,” and be “good for us,” we’ll finally get enough affirmation, enough validation to trust our worth and put down our “me” sword. But it never happens; there is no “enough” point, and so we live in a constant state of lack, always trying to get what we need from the outside so we can be okay on the inside.

Our life becomes an endless project dedicated to self-management.

We feel like we have to be constantly improving the project of "me"—making sure we're doing enough and getting enough. Our life becomes a full-time job of managing the person we're trying to be and be seen as. The result is utter exhaustion and burnout.

Because we experience other people as threats to our self-story, and see others through the lens of whether their behavior serves or doesn’t serve us, we can’t meet people for real, as they are. We’ve got too much skin in the game. Who they are becomes about who they make us feel we are. And so, we can’t really relax fully and get to know others and give them the space to be who they are as whole beings, independent from us, with their own motivations, desires, wants, and needs that are not about us. All roads lead back to us in some way, which clouds our view of the other. We can’t really listen because we have to constantly monitor and scan for potential threats to who we are. We can’t allow others to have a different opinion or experience from us because it “means” our opinion is wrong and consequently, there’s something wrong with us. Our “me” agenda requires everyone else’s thoughts, opinions, and truth to confirm and align with our “me” project, which is a lot of work since that’s never the case. That said, only some parts of other people are allowed into our relationships, the parts that work for us and give us what we need. But we’re not available to meet or know the whole of them.

Our relationships are, therefore, built on filling our own holes and reassuring our own insecurities—getting what we need to feel good or at least okay. We end up using other people to satisfy and validate ourselves. We give in order to feel appreciated and be valued as helpful. We listen to others in order to be perceived as a good listener and so that we can be listened to. How we relate is driven by how it relates to and reflects on us. Our relationships, therefore, can’t be truly open, honest, and emotionally intimate; we can’t be vulnerable and undefended, and can’t really know others as people in their own right, who they really are separate from us. We remain disconnected, relating to others as merely supporting characters in our personal movie—the movie playing in our me-focused mind.

In a recent development, because we’re always telling ourselves a story about our life, what it means for us, whether we’re getting what we need, and whether our life is serving the project of “me,” we’re not available to life as it’s actually happening. We’re not in the present moment; we're trapped inside a story we’ve told ourselves about our life and how our “me” is faring in it. At the same time, we’re not truly connected to other people. Other people are characters in our personal movie, and are experienced through the lens of whether they’re filling our needs and making us feel good about ourselves. Other people are not subjects in their own right, but objects who can help support who we think we are.

It has been revealed that our self-focused approach to life is an attempt to keep us happy and secure, but it ends up backfiring, leaving us feeling disconnected from life and other people, enslaved to how we're being perceived. It leaves us defensive and emotionally fragile, vulnerable to other people’s different opinions and experiences, and having to constantly manage the project of “me” and make sure we’re enough.

In part 3, I’ll dive into the profound benefits of dropping “me” from the center of our universe, and the relief that comes when we learn to show up for life without our “me” in the way, and when we can see life as something happening, but without turning it into something happening to, for, and because of us. What if it’s not about us?

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that WHEN YOUR HOME gym is short on square footage like mine, you need to carefully think about every piece of equipment before it earns its rightful spot. That’s exactly why kettlebells are a staple in my setup. Over time, I’ve built a small but mighty collection—and every single one gets regular use.

A huge perk of kettlebells is that they don’t hog a lot of space (even in a compact home gym) and are relatively inexpensive, notes Tyneka Pack, CPT. These are versatile strength-training tools, too, allowing you to get in a full-body workout, along with explosive power movements, says kettlebell specialist Taylor Beebe, CPT.

As with any fitness equipment, improper use of kettlebells can lead to injury. That’s why most trainers, including Beebe, recommend getting coaching on how to use kettlebells before diving in (peep our how to get started with kettlebell exercises guide).

Like dumbbells, kettlebells come in a wide range of weights, materials, and grips, so it’s crucial to determine which type you’re in the market for before you buy.

It has been revealed that after testing a handful of kettlebells, this cast-iron option from Amazon Basics earns its spot at the top of our list because of its budget price tag and versatile weight options. The weight range from 10 to 60 pounds has allowed me to ramp up my training intensity over time.

This kettlebell has consistently been my go-to and favorite even as I’ve expanded my collection. They’re surprisingly sturdy and durable, even after two years of use. WH fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief also loves this model and has multiple in her home gym, too.

It has been revealed that I own it in several weight sizes, and it has a compact shape that’s great for every kettlebell exercise imaginable. The grip is slightly textured and wide enough to do one- or two-handed exercises, but petite enough for smaller hands like mine. I can confidently hold it, even during potential wall-breaking moves like swings, and it’s comfortable to hold, whether I’m doing one set or five.

Recent findings suggest that while these weights have a lot going for them, there is one con: There is no vinyl coating on the bottom (although there is a vinyl version, which WH editors also love). To avoid scratching my floors, I have to set it down carefully or use a mat underneath.

Many people prefer a competition-style kettlebell due to its uniform design that’s ideal for high reps and technical moves. The Rep Fitness Adjustable Kettlebell offers a competition-style kettlebell shape with adjustable weights, giving you plenty of space-saving mileage out of one tool.

This kettlebell is well-designed, stacking five weights in one relatively compact design. (Weight ranges include 8 to 16 kilograms, 16 to 24 kilograms, and 20 to 40 pounds.) To adjust the weight, just push down on the dial with two fingers, twist to your desired weight, and lift. It has a rubber base to protect your floors although—heads up—the rubber coating is only there when you use the kettlebell’s full weight. Otherwise, you’ll want to set down your kettlebell gingerly.

Recent findings suggest that REP’s adjustable kettlebell is made from cast iron and feels durable. The textured handle is easy to grip and has plenty of space for two-handed moves, although it feels slightly wider than others. If space is a premium at your place and you’re looking to grow with your kettlebell, this is a solid choice.

Read More: Best Compact Home Gym Equipment.

According to recent reports, if you prefer a more traditional competition-style kettlebell, keep scrolling. But if you’re on the hunt for a highly versatile weight that aims to combine the attributes of a kettlebell with those of a dumbbell and a dual-grip medicine ball, the YBell Neo Series is worth consideration.

Recent findings suggest that this weight is perfect for my needs—it’s relatively compact and offers multiple ways to grip, thanks to its unique pyramid-style design. I can use it for everything from biceps curls to lunges, though it’s not ideal for swings.

It has been revealed that the grip on this is perfection. It features a neoprene outer layer to create a slightly sticky feel with impressive gripping power, so I’m not stressed about accidentally flinging it across the room during swings. The wide handle leaves enough room for one- or two-handed exercises, but it may feel a little crowded using both mitts at once if your hands are on the larger side.

Recent findings suggest that you have three different spots you can grip on the outside of this weight, along with an inside bar that’s ideal for dumbbell-style work. While the sides are rounded, I found it was relatively easy to rest the YBell on its base or sides to save space.

The only potential downside of this weight is that it tops out at 26 pounds. If you’re interested in doing heavier lifting, you’ll need to upgrade to a different device.

Industry observers note that A coated kettlebell like this one from Yes4All protects your floors in case of butterfingers through a thoughtfully wrapped coating up the bottom third of the handle. The handle itself makes for a comfortable grip. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi states, “I have the 15-pound model and I never feel it slipping away from me when squatting or doing Russian twists.” It comes in five-pound increments up to 65 pounds, giving you plenty of options.

While I wouldn’t recommend tossing this on your floor at home, the kettlebell doesn’t make a loud noise when it’s dropped, unlike uncoated models. It’s also worth pointing out it’s very affordable, similar to our best overall.Just note the bottom of the kettlebell is not entirely flat, which can be tricky if you’re trying exercises like uneven pushups (with one hand placed through the handles of a KB).

In a recent development, sand kettlebells are a highly portable option that allows you to add a little more instability to your kettlebell workouts. The GoRuck Sand Kettlebell is built tough thanks to its Cordura nylon design and multiple closure system, so you don’t have to stress about accidentally spilling its contents all over the place.

GoRuck’s kettlebell has a teardrop-style shape that works well for many exercises. This kettlebell arrives empty, so you’ll fill it up with sand prior to use. Pro tip: use playground sand available at home improvement stores for this. The reinforcing on nearly all of the seams and bottoms means you can toss this on the ground without worrying about it flying open and spilling sand everywhere.

This style of kettlebell isn’t for everyone, but if you’re looking to add the extra challenge of sandbag training to your kettlebell workouts, this sand kettlebell design will take a lot of abuse and holds up well over time.

“When choosing the correct weight for your kettlebell, it is important to consider your exercise,” says Almoni Ellis, CSCS, CPT. She says that people generally are able to use heavier weights when doing purely lower-body exercises, but that those weights may be too heavy for a person when they’re doing a move like an overhead press, for example.

Recent findings suggest that that said, there’s no one-size-fits-all starting point. Your experience level and current strength come into play, so if you’re unsure where to begin, try testing different weights at a local gym or consider ordering two sizes to see what feels best. As your strength improves, you can gradually increase the weight, adds Pack.

According to recent reports, the most common option for general strength training is the cast-iron kettlebell, which works well for everything from goblet squats to cleans to swings. These are the kettlebells you’ll most often see in home gyms and fitness classes.

Ellis and Pack recommend choosing a cast iron or steel kettlebell because they’re the most durable and long-lasting materials. “Kettlebells [that are] made up of plastic[...] don’t last as long,” Pack states.

According to recent reports, however, most adjustable kettlebells are made with some plastic components, which is necessary for the design. As for vinyl-coated kettlebells, they’re usually made of cast iron with a vinyl coating to prevent damage to floors.

Handle thickness plays a role in both comfort and performance. “Thicker handles can help build grip strength, but they may be more challenging for beginners to control,” claims Pack.

The handle’s coating and texture matter just as much. A slightly textured surface can help you maintain a secure grip, especially during dynamic or high-rep movements. Slick handles, on the other hand, can become slippery as your hands sweat—raising the risk of losing your grip, Pack adds. If you’re training with kettlebell that has a slick grip, consider using workout chalk or liquid chalk during moves like swings.

It has been revealed that to choose the best kettlebells, I consulted three personal trainers who regularly work with kettlebells: Taylor Beebe, CPT, Tyneka Pack, CPT, and Almoni Ellis, CSCS. I also got feedback from Women’s Health fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT, who is a certified trainer.

According to recent reports, based on their feedback, I focused on crucial features to look for in these super versatile strength-training tools. I then tested some of the most popular kettlebells out there. Each was put through a slew of workouts to test its efficiency, durability, weight, material, and grip. Because every person’s budget is different, I made sure to include kettlebells with a range of price points.

South Korea will use emergency alert system to warn about exam cheaters

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters.
  • It has been revealed that officials proposal to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone.
  • The aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

It has been revealed that officials proposal to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

The aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

Korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with new tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

The sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

Industry observers note that days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han indicates he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

Recent findings suggest that “I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student said in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”.

In the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place latest anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin promptly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never mentioned he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

Industry observers note that concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

While fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be upcoming concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an vital role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

Industry observers note that creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.

Here’s a look at some of the best cold-weather gear that will have you wrapping up the gift of warmth and durability… even if that gift is for yourself.

This is an easy gifting win because the warm, hooded, insulated jacket is a recognizable The North Face staple, evoking an unpretentious spin on the brand’s iconic Nuptse Jacket.

This is the perfect type of winter coat: warm but not too puffy.

In a recent development, the Zaneck Jacket is a great alternative to the Aconcagua, stepping away from the outdoorsy look the brand is best known for. It’s still waterproof and insulated, but it has a longer, more modern cut.

The straight cuffs add to its stylish feel in a way that doesn’t scream “I’m dressed for warmth and not fashion,” even though it’s doing both.

According to recent reports, the Lone Peak Triclimate 2 has a lot in common with the Zaneck. From a distance, they cut a similar silhouette. However, the Lone Peak adds a little versatility if you’re looking for a jacket that can handle a variety of climates.

It has been revealed that A removable, insulated inner jacket is attached to a removable, insulated top layer, which is fit for rainy conditions or as a spring or fall jacket. The insulated layer converts the whole thing into a winter-ready jacket. It also sports underarm vents capable of releasing heat in the middle of a long hike, ideal for outdoorsy types. The hood is removable and it’s got adjustable cuffs and an adjustable hem, making this a do-it-all jacket.

Sources indicate that it might be easy to ignore the Pertex Jacket. It’s a bit unassuming. It doesn’t cut as stylish of a figure as the Zaneck, but it’s endlessly useful. The lightweight Pertex fabric will keep you dry in a downpour, but it also offers warmth without marshmallow-like bulk.

In a recent development, the lightweight aspect makes this the kind of coat you toss in the backseat on the way to a hike, just in case. It’s also great for layering, whether it’s tossed on over a sweater or layered under an overcoat to make a favorite jacket more winter-ready.

In a recent development, this edition of the classic Base Camp Duffel echoes the design details we love in The North Face’s jackets. While it’s got enough style and a heap of color options for daily use, it’s built for adventure.

Tech Report: Bob Hope at Home: 10 Photos of the Comic’s Life Behind the Curtain

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though Bob Hope was born in England, he fell in love with the USA.
  • Sources indicate that born Leslie Townes Hope in Eltham, London, on May 29, 1903, the future comedian and actor came from humble beginnings.
  • Below, we’ve rounded up 10 photos of Hope at home, from his early family life to the residence where he died at age 100.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though Bob Hope was born in England, he fell in love with the USA. “Sometimes I do my best to hide it, but I’ve got a real crush on America,” he wrote in his 1990 memoir, Don’t Shoot, It’s Only Me. “Nobody ever had a girl like her. Nobody ever gave me as much affection, as much honor, or as much real estate.”.

Sources indicate that born Leslie Townes Hope in Eltham, London, on May 29, 1903, the future comedian and actor came from humble beginnings. His family had little money and moved often throughout his childhood. After he found success on stage and it came time to raise his own brood, Hope put down roots in California. Across Toluca Lake and Palm Springs, the star’s homes offered a place to escape the limelight, spend time with his wife and four kids, entertain very famous guests, and indulge in his love of golf.

Below, we’ve rounded up 10 photos of Hope at home, from his early family life to the residence where he died at age 100.

Industry observers note that hope (bottom right) at the family estate in Cleveland. The comic’s parents William Henry Hope and Avis Townes Hope are on the porch in the background. Hope was 20 years old at the time of the picture.

According to recent reports, hope and his family moved from London to the United States when he was four. In this 1923 photo, he’s pictured with friends and members of the Hope clan at their Cleveland home. Because money was tight, the family took in boarders to supplement Hope’s father’s income, according to the Library of Congress. In his 1954 memoir, Have Tux, Will Travel, Hope recalls his early days in Cleveland. “The first place we lived by ourselves was Standiforth Court,” he wrote. “We were always on the move. We lived at 2029 Euclid. After that we moved behind the Cleveland Express barns…. It was a long walk between the barns and our house. And if we got home after dark, it was scary…. Next we lived at 1925 East 105th, then at 1913, then at 2029—all on Euclid. We didn’t move very far, only to bigger houses which had more room for roomers.”.

Hope and his wife Dolores at home in the 1940s.

In a recent development, hope married Dolores DeFina in 1934, and the couple adopted their first child, a daughter named Linda, in 1939. That same year, the comic bought a five-acre former walnut grove in Los Angeles’s Toluca Lake neighborhood at 10346 Moorpark Street. He transformed the property into a lavish French Revival estate, featuring a 14,876-square-foot main house with eight bedrooms and eight bathrooms; a two-bedroom, two-bathroom guesthouse; a staff residence; and a pool.

Hope and his grandfather catch up over tea.

In this 1943 photo, Hope is pictured at home with his “Grandpop.” As a young boy in London, Hope lived with his family in a house his grandfather had built. “Grandpop had built a row of houses in Eltham. We lived in one of them. They were put together like stone battleships,” he writes in Have Tux, Will Travel. After moving to the United States, his grandfather went on to build churches in Cleveland and Detroit. Hope reunited with him during a return trip to England in 1939—the star’s first visit since moving across the pond as a child. He recalls the occasion in his memoir, writing that “It wasn’t until I went back to England in 1939 that I got to know [Grandpop]. It was the first time I’d been there since I was four. The English papers reported: ‘One-time shoeshine boy and ironmonger’s assistant comes home.’ The English are supposed to be conservative and not given to exaggeration, but they hooked one there. How could I have been a shoeshine boy or ironmonger’s assistant when I was only four when I left there?”.

Hope and family at home in the 1940s.

Back in California, Hope and his wife continued to grow their family. They adopted three more children: Anthony, born in 1940, and twins William and Eleanora, born in 1946. In this circa 1940s photo, the family of six is pictured at home. In Have Tux, Will Travel, Hope reflects on the choice to adopt. “No matter how strongly I feel about the word ‘family,’ Dolores feels even more deeply about it,” he writes. “When we found out that she couldn’t bear children, she began to bend my ear about adoption.” They welcomed their children through The Cradle, an adoption agency in Evanston, Illinois. “Of the five thousand, four hundred and nine babies that The Cradle has placed, there are eight Cradle babies out here in Hollywood,” he continues. “The Hopes are proud to be Cradle parents. I wish I could really tell you what The Cradle means to me here in Hollywood, where all day long the talk is box-office and autographs and premieres and who’ll get the Oscar. ‘The town of make-believe,’ they call it, but don’t get the idea everything is make-believe in Hollywood. There's nothing make-believe about our children. They are real.”.

Hope enjoys some family time in the living room with Dolores and two of their children.

In a recent development, hope’s Toluca Lake estate was more than a family retreat; it was also a gathering place for celebrities and politicians, including Bing Crosby and Richard Nixon. When the property went on the market for $27.5 million in 2013, listing agent Jade Mills noted, “[Hope’s] daughter, Linda Hope, would often peek down the grand staircase to see who was coming. She once spoke to Lucie Arnaz and Maria Cooper about doing a book about watching celebrities come and go called ‘Seen From the Landing.’”.

Sources indicate that the home was “always impressively staffed,” Mills continued. “A full-time cook, butler, estate manager, and two housekeepers manned the property on a daily basis, while additional staff was hired for large receptions.”.

Hope, Dolores, and their four kids pose at home in 1958.

In this 1958 photo, Hope and the family pose for a photo on the stairs. In Have Tux, Will Travel, the comic gushes about his wife as a mother. “Dolores has a wise and loving touch with our children,” he writes. “I’m lost in admiration of the job she has done with them, and with the job she’s done with keeping me in line. A lot of children whose fathers are in show business grow up too precocious, too wise, too fresh, too unfunny. That’s not true of our four. Dolores sees to that. She also sees to it that they’re having a devout rearing.”.

The family is shown here opening Christmas presents in 1964.

Hope was determined to give his children space at home. “When our kids began to grow up, we fixed up a play room for them and gave them rooms of their own,” he writes in Have Tux, Will Travel. “While we were at it, Dolores and I decided to redo the whole house. We tore out one entire downstairs wall and put in glass, so no matter where we are, we can look out at the garden and enjoy the California sun—if it reveals up.”.

It has been revealed that while his home workspace was connected to the residence, it was its own separate world. “My office adjoins my house,” he writes. “It’s a different project, separate and distinct from our house. In fact, it’s on a different property. It was put up (and is owned) by Hope Enterprises. But it’s handy. The people I want to see on business can walk in and out without disturbing anybody…. It’s a nice set-up.”.

Hope was an avid golfer in his free time.

In a recent development, hope was an avid golfer and built a one-hole golf course at his home in Toluca Lake, where he’s pictured here in this 1990-era photo. He once even mentioned that he considered golf to be his real job. “Golf is my profession,” he said, per ESPN. “Entertainment is just a sideline. I tell jokes to pay my greens fees.” The outlet further reported that he played more than 2,000 courses all over the world and golfed with everyone from Crosby to Dwight Eisenhower and Bill Clinton. “I’ve played all over the world, which means there isn’t a country with a course in which I haven’t three-putted,” Hope said.

Hope and Dolores at home in Palm Springs.

While Toluca Lake served as the family’s primary residence, Hope’s most iconic home was arguably his Palm Springs estate, where he and Dolores are pictured here in 1991. Designed by famed architect John Lautner, the 24,000-square-foot estate featured 10 bedrooms, dramatic arches, and a statement curved roof. The futuristic design closely resembled a spaceship. Hope once joked, “Well, at least when they come down from Mars they’ll know where to go.”.

The home’s construction, however, was plagued by setbacks. According to the Los Angeles Times, when building began in the early ’70s, the structure caught on fire and burned down. The project was subsequently delayed for five years, during which time the couple’s interior designer, Arthur Elrod, was killed in a car accident. Dolores then took over the design duties. Lautner’s protégé Helena Arahuete recalled Dolores’s vision: “She wanted everything very ornamented, very rich—you know, gold and pink and black and mirrors everywhere.” Inspired by her friends Walter and Leonore Annenberg’s home, which had a pink roof, Dolores requested that their curved roof be covered in pink terra-cotta gunite.

In 1991, at his Palm Springs pad, Hope hosted “Bob Hope’s Yellow Ribbon Party,” a homecoming celebration for U.S. troops. The soiree included celebrity guest appearances by Brooke Shields, Patti LaBelle, Jimmy Stewart, and former President Gerald Ford and his wife, Betty.

Recent findings suggest that hope died at home in Toluca Lake in 2003 at the age of 100. The estate remained in the family until Dolores’s death in 2011, after which it was listed for $50 million. LA businessman Ron Burkle purchased the star’s Palm Springs pad in 2016, and two years later, added Hope’s Toluca Lake residence to his real estate portfolio.

Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1382 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.
  • The reports detail how cardiovascular health complications can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.
  • The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health complications can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

They stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

The authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” mentioned Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”.

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, noted the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these new reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah said.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”.

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg mentioned this life-stage breakdown is key, especially for risk reduction.

Sources indicate that she noted issues with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg said.

It has been revealed that suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”.

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” said Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”.

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

“These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”.

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are crucial windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” said William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”.

According to recent reports, the authors note several age-related warning signs of heart problems. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” noted Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”.

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

Sources indicate that the authors of that report listed several steps they said could reverse these trends. Among them:.

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:.

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu said.

Industry observers note that weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She said that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Khan remarked women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”.

#110514. Latest Update: The Boon of Being Highly Sensitive

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1535 w)

Latest Update: The Boon of Being Highly Sensitive

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1535 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Are you more easily overstimulated than others by what’s going on around you?
  • In a recent development, we all navigate the world using our senses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Are you more easily overstimulated than others by what’s going on around you? Maybe you’re easily distracted or stressed by loud noises (it’s the kitchen exhaust fan for me), bright artificial lighting, uncomfortable clothing, or other people’s moods. If so, you may be among the 30% of people who are highly sensitive to sensory input from the environment.

In a recent development, we all navigate the world using our senses. It’s just that some of us seem to take in more and be more impacted by what we take in. Scientists are still making discoveries about sensory processing in different situations and for different people.

Industry observers note that here’s a fascinating example — did you know that human hands can sense the presence of something without touching it? Last year, a group of researchers published the first study demonstrating remote sensing in humans (Chen, Crucianelli, Versace, & Jamone, 2025). Participants in their study were able to detect that an object was buried in sand when their fingers were still 6.9 cm away from the object. How? Humans can perceive subtle changes in the sand caused by the object. What’s even more incredible is that humans were 30% more accurate than robotic sensors. Specifically, the robotic sensors had more false positives (“sensing” an object when there was not one). The researchers suspect humans are better able to interpret touch sensations because our nervous systems are designed to filter noise, weigh uncertainty, and make decisions about ambiguous situations.

Sources indicate that clearly, there's still a lot to learn about sensory processing in humans. These days, it’s widely accepted that some of us are more sensitive to the environment than others. As we understand more about sensory sensitivity, more research is focusing on an idea intuitive to many of us: sensory processing sensitivity comes with great benefits.

Dr. Elaine Aron began researching sensory processing sensitivity (SPS; also called high sensitivity) in 1991. SPS is well summarized as “lower sensory thresholds, susceptibility to overstimulation, deeper processing of environmental information, heightened emotional and physiological reactivity, and increased awareness of subtle stimuli” (Weyn, Greven, Schmidt, Gillebert, 2025).

SPS isn't a diagnosis. It's a normally distributed personality trait or aspect of temperament. This means we all fall somewhere on the sensitivity continuum. While 20-30% of us are highly sensitive, 40-50% of us are moderately sensitive, and 20-30% of us have low sensitivity (Lionetti et al. 2018). Evolutionary theories suggest there is an advantage for humans if some of us (not too many) are highly sensitive (Greven et al. 2019).

Sources indicate that sensory sensitivity is heritable. Studies have found that 47% of the variability in sensory sensitivity is explained by genetics (Assary, 2020). It’s also biologically based. Neuroimaging studies have found that folks with SPS have greater activation in brain areas involved in sensory processing (e.g., awareness, integration, empathy, preparation for action, higher-order visual processing).

In a recent development, sensory processing sensitivity is typically measured using the Highly Sensitive Person Scale, which was revised earlier this year (Pluess et al. 2026). It's an 18-item questionnaire that captures six domains of sensitivity: 1. sensitivity to details 2. depth of processing 3. social sensitivity 4. sensitivity to positive experiences 5. emotional reactivity and 6. overstimulation.

Sources indicate that if you (or someone you’re close to) has high sensory sensitivity, you don’t need me to tell you about its challenges, which can include overstimulation, exhaustion, and stress. What might not be top of mind are the benefits that can come along with high SPS. You may be surprised to learn that folks who have high SPS may actually be better positioned to thrive in supportive, positive environments (Damatac et al. 2025).

Recent findings suggest that if you’re someone who is more easily overstimulated by unpleasant sensory input like the kitchen fan, you’re likely also more easily positively influenced by positive input such as a view of the gorgeous fall leaves. And the positive benefit is likely to be longer-lasting. This makes logical sense. It’s also been supported by the research. In one example, Lionette et al. (2018) found that folks who had high SPS had a more positive response to happy video clips as compared with people who had lower sensory sensitivity. Research has also found that folks with high SPS can actually experience more benefit from psychological interventions and social support as compared with people with lower SPS (Damatac, et al. 2025; Nocentini, Menesini, & Pluess 2018).

Industry observers note that this sensitivity to positive experiences overlaps with another dimension of SPS — aesthetic sensitivity. Aesthetic sensitivity describes the deep emotional and physiological response to beauty, art, and nature often experienced by folks who are highly sensitive.

Chacón et al. (2024) found aesthetic sensitivity among folks with high SPS strongly correlated with the personality traits openness and agreeableness (a replication of previous findings), as well as adaptive coping strategies including emotional expression and regulation. They found that folks with high SPS and high aesthetic sensitivity more effectively navigated emotionally dysregulating challenges in daily living, such as problematic situations at work.

Recent findings suggest that another recent study found that folks with sensory sensitivity demonstrated higher cognitive flexibility, which is associated with adaptive coping and problem-solving (Shippers, Hoogman & Greven, 2025). The study also found that folks with high SPS who were more sensitive to aesthetic beauty scored higher on measures of curiosity and humor.

If you’re highly sensitive, you're likely more inclined toward creativity and empathy. Laros-van Gorkom et al. (2025) found that folks with high sensory sensitivity are more likely to be more empathic and more likely to have creative ideas. In their study, folks with high aesthetic sensitivity were more likely to engage in creative activities.

It has been revealed that those of us who have high sensory sensitivity experience awe more frequently. For example, Dunne et al (2024) found that folks with high SPS were more likely to experience a profound emotional and physiological response to the beauty of nature. This experience of awe directs attention away from ourselves and toward our natural surroundings, which deepens our connection to the natural world. The experience of awe is widely known to enhance well-being.

This rally around the advantages of SPS is extremely encouraging. It confirms that sensory sensitivity can be a strength promoting well-being. In positive environments, folks with SPS are actually uniquely positioned to flourish.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • IONNA, the DC charging operator backed by several major OEMs, has opened its largest DC charging site yet, with 22 bays of 400kW charging in Westminster, California.
  • Alongside the opening, IONNA is also enabling Plug & Charge operation for Tesla EVs, with Stellantis EVs “coming soon.”.
  • IONNA is a rapidly expanding DC charging network which is garnering good reviews from EV drivers, with clean, fast and easy to use charging stations (which it calls “Rechargeries”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IONNA, the DC charging operator backed by several major OEMs, has opened its largest DC charging site yet, with 22 bays of 400kW charging in Westminster, California.

Alongside the opening, IONNA is also enabling Plug & Charge operation for Tesla EVs, with Stellantis EVs “coming soon.”.

IONNA is a rapidly expanding DC charging network which is garnering good reviews from EV drivers, with clean, fast and easy to use charging stations (which it calls “Rechargeries”).

Recent findings suggest that but until now, we haven’t had all that many chargers in the LA area. There are a couple in South OC and the Inland Empire, but nothing closer to the population center of the metro area (though more are opening soon).

That changes now with IONNA’s newly introduced flagship charging station in Westminster. It features 12 CCS connectors and 10 NACS ports, so you can charge just about any EV (no Chademo, nor can my AC-only Tesla Roadster charge here… ho hum).

In addition to 22 chargers with peak 400kW capacity, the site features indoor and outdoor lounge space, restrooms, and other amenities like an In N Out and a taco shop across the street. (Not quite as full-featured as my favorite charging station, Rove, but IONNA has a much larger national footprint, and does have faster chargers).

Industry observers note that there’s also a small, convenience-store-like area that uses Amazon’s “just walk out” technology. You swipe a card to unlock the room, pick up any items you want, and just walk out. The many cameras on the ceiling track you (and whoever came in with you) and what you’re picking up, then charge your card for the items you took with you.

The store has snacks and drinks, though no ice cream, which is the main thing I’m looking for on a roadtrip stop… IONNA may convert one of the fridges to a freezer in the future, depending on how things go.

And, importantly, the site has trash cans and window wipers – just what you need on a roadtrip stop.

Speaking of roadtrips, the charger opening caps off a cross-country roadtrip by IONNA personnel, who set out in several cars from various parts of the country, all convening on the upcoming Rechargery in Westminster.

Over 20 EVs joined the roadtrip and drove over 40,000 combined miles on their trip to Westminster. The teams charged at approximately 30% of the firm’s charging sites, showing just how easy it is to do roadtrips in an EV.

Recent findings suggest that the Rechargery opens tomorrow in Westminster, at 6260 Westminster Blvd, just off the 405 freeway. Look for the substantial sign. For the first weeks, you can charge at a promotional rate of $0.20/kWh. Afterwards, IONNA will charge its standard rate of $0.39/kWh.

Perhaps more importantly than a upcoming charger opening, though, is IONNA’s announcement today that Teslas can now use its network with Plug & Charge functionality (well, technically Autocharge, which is basically the same thing).

Window wipers and fluid are an underrated missing feature at EV stations, hope to see more of this.

What this means is that you can link your car and credit card ahead of time (via the Presto charging app), then simply plug in at any IONNA station and start charging, without having to tap or swipe or open an app. This is similar to the experience Teslas have always had on Superchargers, so should be familiar to Tesla owners.

In a recent development, the functionality is rolled out across all of IONNA’s network, starting today. So you should be able to test it out on your Tesla vehicle. IONNA already supports Plug & Charge for BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Rivian, Ford, Porsche and Volvo EVs.

Further, IONNA claims support is “coming soon” for Stellantis EVs (Jeep, Dodge, Ram, Fiat), stating that those cars will be able to Plug & Charge on its network in December. It now supports Autocharge for about two thirds of the EVs on American roads.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that UPDATE, November 19, 2026, 4:15 p.m. EST: Fiona the hippo has died.

Fiona the hippo remains under the watchful eyes of veterinarians and staff at the Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing a hat last week. As a full-grown hippo, surgery is not an option for Fiona, but her caretakers remain hopeful she will pass the foreign object naturally.

Last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remains stuck in her digestive track. She has undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that show intestinal bunching, indicating her body is continuing to try and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests.

In a recent development, “Fiona ingested an object that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat,” the Cincinnati Zoo said in a statement. “Our veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely. Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self. Fiona will remain off habitat until this is resolved. We will share updates as we have more information.”.

Recent findings suggest that the zoo also reminded patrons to be careful with their things when observing animals: “Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately.”.

Sources indicate that on Wednesday, November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the team explained.

In a recent development, fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix is one of the most glamorous weekends in sports. With drivers’ global followings and a long list of A-listers in attendance, the event can feel as much like a fashion show as a race.

But while many guests were focused on the designer labels, Kristin Juszczyk had another message in mind: the need for more research on women in sports.

Juszczyk is a self-taught designer whose work began as a hobby and has since made her a force in the industry. The wife of San Francisco 49ers player Kyle Juszczyk, her custom game-day outfits gained traction on social media, and she has gone on to dress high-profile names including Simone Biles, Taylor Swift, and Caitlin Clark. This year, she was also named to TIME’s 100 Most Influential People in Sports.

For the Las Vegas GP, Juszczyk partnered with Gatorade’s Body of Science, an initiative dedicated to advancing the research on women’s sports. One stat drives their research: 6 percent of sports science research focuses on women.

Only 6 percent of published research in sports and exercise journals has focused exclusively on women, per a study published in the Women in Sport and Physical Activity Journal—a staggering gap that has implications for everything from training to recovery, as previously reported by Women’s Health.

Tennis legend Venus Williams, a Gatorade athlete, wore a custom look Juszczyk designed for the paddock red carpet inspired by this staggering statistic.

“Venus is one of the most iconic athletes of our generation, and to have her being in one of my designs, is surreal,” Juszczyk exclusively tells Women’s Health.

When it came to building the design, Juszczyk notes she first took inspiration from motorsport fashion while also channeling the ambience a city like Las Vegas brings to the race. She opted to use leather as the base material, feeling like it channeled the energy of the sport. From there, she designed a trench coat with a layering corset piece over it, an homage to the city’s glitz and glamour.

Designing a trench coat was a first for Juszczyk, but the corset design is what she describes as her personal “bread and butter.” True to the Gatorade brand, the trench featured piping in its iconic orange, offset with black.

That 6 percent statistic is also front and center, ensuring the message of the design is clear: There needs to be more research dedicated toward women’s sports.

In a recent development, juszczyk wanted to stay true to Venus and her personal style, and did a lot of research on what she wears on the regular. She says she approaches all of her designs with intentionality, ensuring the client is wearing something they feel good in.

“I want it to feel like my design, but I still want it to be something they feel beautiful and confident in,” she says.

The look was on full display when Venus presented the winner of the F1 Academy race, Alisha Palmowski, with her trophy. The moment was symbolic: a titan of women’s sports celebrating the new generation, while calling attention to a research gap that directly affects them.

It has been revealed that “If anyone can take anything away from it, it’s that women need as much research in sports as men do,” she says. “The world is doing so much in pushing women athletes forward, and science should back it as well.”.

Alyssa Cruz is the social media editor at Women’s Health, where she drives social strategy and helps shape the brand’s voice across platforms. Prior to WH, she worked at CBS News and palabra. Originally from Toledo, she is a proud alumna of Ohio University, where she received two bachelor’s degrees in journalism and Spanish. When she is not creating social content, you can find her trying different restaurants in Latest York City or planning her next trip.

BYD is preparing to launch a fresh midsize SUV under its personalized, off-road-focused sub-brand. The new SUV was spotted testing, offering an early look at its boxy, rugged-looking design.

Fang Cheng Bao, or FCB as many call it, is another BYD sub-brand, alongside Denza and Yangwang.

The “personalization-focused” brand offers a lineup of hardcore electric and plug-in hybrid SUVs, including the Bao 5 and Bao 8, sold as the Denza B5 and B8 outside of China.

In a recent development, it also sells the Tai series, designed more as everyday family vehicles, such as the Tai 7. BYD sells the Tai 7 as the Ti 7 under its own brand in Europe and the UK, where Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has taken legal action, alleging it’s a copycat of the Defender.

Meanwhile, BYD is gearing up to add another SUV to the lineup. FCB’s general manager, Xiong Tianbo, previously confirmed that the Tai 6, or Ti 6, will launch in 2027.

Ahead of its official debut, the new Ti 6 was captured in China. Although it’s still covered, the images sent to Autohome suggest it retains the boxy, upright design of the larger Ti 7 but appears slightly smaller.

Unlike the Ti 7’s split-headlight design, the smaller SUV features redesigned headlights. Like most of BYD’s new higher-end vehicles, the SUV is equipped with a LiDAR to support advanced safety and convenience features.

BYD has not revealed battery or powertrain specs, but the Ti 6 (Tai 6) is expected to be offered in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) variants.

Sources indicate that it will likely offer a similar setup to the Ti 7. The Ti 7 PHEV uses a 1.5L engine and an electric motor that delivers a combined 360 kW (482 hp).

The pure electric version with a single motor delivers 300 kW (402 hp), while the dual-motor variant delivers 515 kW (690 hp).

Since the Tai 7 (Ti 7) starts at 179,800 yuan ($27,000), the smaller Tai 6 (Ti 6) will likely be priced in the 150,00 yuan ($22,500) range.

In a recent development, if you’re into personal audio, you might not want to spend all your money during Black Friday/Cyber Monday (but feel free to spend a little, and keep coming back here for some great suggestions as to how). Just within the last week, several innovative latest headphones and earbuds have been announced, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

First up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the fresh Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

In a recent development, the 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

Both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously announced $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

Compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned company expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

It has been revealed that being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

It has been revealed that as for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

Over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the company has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

Recent findings suggest that the overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the firm’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

To ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.
