📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every year, millions of people line the streets of Newly introduced York City or tune in at home to watch the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, but few people know the ins and outs of the full-time, year-round work that makes the spectacle possible. In honor of the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, Hoda Kotb, who has hosted the event since 2018, brought AD for a look inside the 72,000-square-foot studio where all of the floats, balloons, and costumes are designed and constructed. Read on to discover the most interesting behind-the-scenes tidbits that we learned.

Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

According to recent reports, “Everything you see in the parade is done right here in the studio,” indicates executive producer Will Coss, showing off the massive warehouse where more than 75 people, spread across costume, sculpting, metal shop, engineering, carpentry, and balloon fabrication departments, work a collective 50,000 hours each year. Before the Macy’s team moved into their current space, the magic happened inside a former Tootsie Roll factory in Hoboken, New Jersey.

Hoda Kotb and Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade executive producer Will Coss.

The first parade in 1924 featured animals from the Central Park zoo, including elephants, lions, tigers, and bears. They were soon replaced with the giant character balloons that the parade is famous for today, but even that tradition used to look different. From 1928 to 1932, the balloons were released into the air and people were encouraged to find them for a cash reward. “That went on until things got a bit more challenging in the skies, because private aircraft would actually go and track them and try to grab them and bring them back down to Earth,” explains Coss. “But in 1931, there was a blue hippo that was released, never to be seen again. And this year, the blue hippo is making his triumphant return back to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.”.

In addition to the blue hippo, balloons of yore will be making a comeback for the 100th parade, including Felix the Cat, the first character balloon to appear in the parade, and Underdog, who hasn’t made an appearance at the parade in 42 years. Snoopy, the most frequently recurring balloon, will return this year as his alter ego Joe Cool for the first time.

Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

It has been revealed that “The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been in production since my first day here, five years ago,” says Coss. “This year the stakes are high; you only have one shot at the 100th.” To mark the occasion, there will be seven latest balloons, six new floats, and one new “balloonicle,” or balloon vehicle.

Hoda Kotb welcoming AD to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

Recent findings suggest that from concept drawings to weatherproofing, it can take up to six months to complete a parade float. “While a lot of the work here requires a lot of planning, a lot of design, a lot of engineering, our end goal is to bring people together, to inspire joy, to create that latest tradition,” says Coss, “whether it’s a family experiencing it for the first time or experiencing it for the 25th time.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that WE’D ALL LIKE to imagine our hair as strong, resilient, healthy. And there’s no shortage of products marketed toward reaching that end point. You’ve got your bond-building treatments, your protein masks, your strengthening serums—heck, there are now entire product lines geared toward promoting robust, rugged strands.

But what exactly does it mean to have ‘strong’ hair?

Industry observers note that we tend to equate strength with the kind of glossy, thick, bouncy strands you'd see in a shampoo commercial. But there’s more to the science than that. For starters, hair that looks healthy isn't necessarily strong, and hair that's naturally fine or thinning isn't automatically weak. Plus, there's a difference between making hair “feel” stronger and actually improving its ability to withstand breakage.

Meet the experts: Sherry Maragh, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist based in Virginia. Nathan Puksta is the founder and CEO of FILAMENT Sciences, a haircare brand focused on the science of stronger hair.

So, what counts as strong hair, and can all these products really deliver on their promises? We asked two experts to explain.

Scientifically speaking, hair strength is all about resilience, meaning how well an individual strand withstands stress from brushing, stretching, styling, and other everyday activities without breaking. That strength largely comes from two parts of the hair shaft: the cuticle, which acts as its protective outer layer, and the cortex, which contains keratin proteins responsible for much of its structural integrity, explains Sherry Maragh, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Virginia.

Another notable factor is elasticity, or the ability of hair to stretch and return toward its original shape without snapping. One of the most useful measurements is tensile strength, which quantifies how much force a strand can withstand before breaking, claims Nathan Puksta, the founder and CEO of FILAMENT Sciences, which creates products and ingredients dedicated to the science of stronger hair. Think of it as the difference between a brittle piece of dry spaghetti and a flexible rubber band.

Tensile strength is an vital part of this conversation because it’s something that laboratories can actually measure, using calibrated equipment that pulls individual hair fibers until they break. Other tests evaluate elasticity, breakage, and resistance to combing. But strength isn't synonymous with thickness, density, or shine. "Hair can absolutely be strong while still being fine, thin, or less reflective," says Dr. Maragh. "Similarly, hair that appears thick and glossy is not necessarily resistant to breakage." In other words, those naturally fine strands might be remarkably resilient, while locks that epitomize the “glass hair” trend could be surprisingly fragile.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, the things we regularly do to make our hair look good can also compromise its strength. Puksta identifies five major contributors to weakened hair: chemical processing, mechanical damage, heat, environmental exposure, and aging.

According to recent reports, chemical treatments, particularly bleaching and certain straightening processes, can be especially damaging because they alter the hair's internal structure. But everyday habits matter, too. Those can look like:.

So, can you actually make your hair stronger? Yes, but there's an important distinction between improving damaged hair's performance and returning it to its original, undamaged condition. "The visible hair shaft is made up of nonliving cells, so damaged hair cannot biologically heal in the way skin does," claims Dr. Maragh.

That doesn't mean strengthening products are useless. Certain ingredients can improve hair's physical properties, reduce friction, reinforce weakened areas, and help prevent additional breakage, with some technologies even working beneath the cuticle. Puksta explains that bond-building treatments target chemical interactions within hair, while certain peptides and proteins can help reinforce its keratin structure. However, effectiveness varies considerably between formulations.

According to recent reports, dr. Maragh cautions that an ingredient's ability to penetrate the hair shaft doesn't automatically prove that it repairs structural damage. So, what can different strengthening products realistically accomplish?

And remember that a product claiming 80 percent stronger hair isn't necessarily saying what you think. Dr. Maragh recommends examining what was measured, the comparison group, and whether results came from laboratory testing or consumer feedback. Protein retention, for example, isn't the same measurement as tensile strength.

Pantene Abundant & Strong Shampoo.

Sources indicate that A 2026 Women’s Beauty Award winner, this wash is prized for its ability to deeply hydrate and help detangle, cutting down on pulling while brushing. It also contains ingredients that battle oxidative stress on the scalp, helping follicles hang onto hair for longer.

According to recent reports, A solid conditioner that helps detangle and cut down on styling damage is worth its weight in gold. Dove’s product contains a peptide complex that helps to repair damage.

Oribe Hair Alchemy Fortifying Treatment Serum.

Sources indicate that this serum contains a curative complex of chia seed, plant protein, and bio-fermented bamboo leaf that the brand claims can penetrate the cortex to heal from within. But perhaps its biggest plus is that it can protect hair from heat damage up to 450 degrees.

FILAMENT TS.02/Tt: Tensile Strength Hair Treatment Mask.

Featuring a patented complex that improves hairs’ tensile strength, this mask also contains a plant oil blend for moisturization and protection.

In a small study conducted by the brand, this biotin-free bioactive blend was shown to support hair density and thickness.

Here's the good news: You don't need naturally thick, glossy hair to have strong hair. And if your strands are damaged, there are meaningful ways to improve their resilience. The key is understanding what products can—and cannot—accomplish. A conditioner that reduces breakage through easier detangling is valuable, even if it doesn't rebuild internal bonds. Likewise, a treatment that improves measurable tensile strength isn't necessarily reversing every aspect of previous damage (translation: it can’t recreate virgin hair).

Industry observers note that ultimately, maintaining strength is as much about preventing damage as treating it. Consistent conditioning, gentler styling practices, and choosing products suited to your hair type can help protect existing strands while healthy latest hair grows.

And that's worth remembering the next time you see a bottle that promises stronger hair: The goal is helping the strands withstand whatever you put them through—not just have shampoo commercial-worthy hair.

  • According to recent reports, charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to new research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

According to recent reports, charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

According to recent reports, the findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, said Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she remarked.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz stated the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

According to recent reports, she remarked researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”.

Industry observers note that weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he remarked. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

Sources indicate that “It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy mentioned.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy remarked. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham stated the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

Sources indicate that the study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also said the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham said adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so vital,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive proposal,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:.

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England. Even more exciting, CCTV cameras captured the poignant moment for this threatened species. The footage shows rhino mom Asha giving birth, and the calf’s first unsure steps into the world.

The sex and weight have not been declared yet, and the calf also does not have a name.

Industry observers note that at birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds. By comparison, the largest adult greater one-horned rhinos weigh over two tons, or as much as a car.

The team used a combination of experience and non-invasive testing to help strategy out the pregnancy. They closely monitored Asha’s behavior and regularly collected samples of her poop. By testing hormone levels in the samples, they could track Asha’s reproductive cycle and identify when she would be most open to mating. This helped the team safely introduce her to Beni the rhino, while a separate analysis helped confirm the pregnancy.

In a recent development, “Asha was pregnant for about 15 months, so it’s a long wait! We had our fingers crossed when she indicated signs of labour and we knew we were likely to welcome the calf very soon,” Emma Evison, Team Manager for rhinos said in an e-mailed statement. “It was a major moment for us—and for the conservation breeding programme—when the calf arrived. Any birth can be risky, even for an experienced mum, but fortunately everything went smoothly. The calf was up and about within an hour and feeding shortly afterwards. Asha knows exactly what she’s doing.”.

It has been revealed that both mother and calf are reportedly in good health. They remained inside for the first few days following the birth to stay warm, but are now venturing to a special behind-the-scenes paddock outside of the enclosure. The calf is Asha’s fourth with father Beni. Sadly, Beni died in September following a sudden and brief illness.

Recent findings suggest that “Beni was a lovely rhino. He was calm and approachable, helped train animal care specialists and even took part in animal behaviour studies,” added Tom Garland, Assistant Manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf.”.

Industry observers note that while not the largest rhino species in the world, greater one-horned rhinos stand about six feet tall at the shoulder and are the biggest in Asia. They have the smallest horns of any rhino, but also have the biggest teeth. The males will sometimes use these chompers to bite each other while sparring. At the moment, about 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos are alive today. They live in India and Nepal, in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. In the early 1990s, trophy hunting and habitat loss almost drove them to extinction.. Poaching for their prized horns also threatened their survival.

Sources indicate that while the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species presently lists them as Vulnerable, they remain  at risk of extinction. Many of the rhinos are concentrated into a relatively small number of protected areas, putting their genetic diversity at risk. A lack of genetic diversity can lead to inbreeding and worse health outcomes in general. This newly introduced calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding program to help maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos living in human care.

Industry observers note that “Supporting Asha’s pregnancy has been really exciting,” added conservation scientist John O’Hanlan. “She’s one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is notable in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

In a recent development, grand Theft Auto VI has been dominating the lives of gamers, young and old, since its arrival on November 19th. It can seem impossible for parents to resist the inertia that settles on kids as they spend dozens (hundreds) of hours in front of screens engaged in violent role-play. While there is no easy solution, with the holidays fast approaching and gift-giving on many parents' minds, maybe there is a quaint solution to this very technological problem. Knitting.

In a recent development, A few months ago I was presenting to an audience in northern Norway where I observed something odd. At least 10% of my audience were knitting. These weren’t church ladies with white hair and compression socks (what an awful stereotype but sadly one that is portrayed far too often in our popular culture). My audience of knitters comprised, instead, younger women and men who were listening attentively to what I was saying while occupying their hands with needles and skeins of yarn. Where it has become routine to put stress balls and fidget toys on conference room tables, here was a much nicer way to evoke calm. Even better, the repetition wasn’t a wasted act of self-flagellation. My audience was engaged in a creative activity that turned a ball of wool into gifts for children or casual sofa throws for lovers and friends.

Why don’t we teach children to knit anymore? For that matter, why has it become so rare to see a child whittling with a pocket knife, sewing, building a tree fort, painting their room, drawing a tree, or creating something that is three-dimensional, tactile? So few children experience a distraction that has purpose and a tangible outcome. Video games are the opposite. Time consuming with no discernible gain.

It has been revealed that if this sounds like nonsensical nostalgia, it’s not. There is good reason to believe that one part of the solution to our children’s mental health crisis is to be found in encouraging them to do arts and crafts and other do-it-yourself (DIY) activities like woodwork and gardening. In a study of 18-24-year-olds recruited (ironically) online, those who were more engaged in extracurricular activities, including crafts, reported significantly lower risk for suicide and a greater sense of belongingness, two outcomes that are co-dependent.

That same pattern was found during the COVID-19 pandemic when some 3,725 adults were surveyed in the USA, with a clear pattern to the findings. Those who gardened, those who did woodwork, and those who immersed themselves regularly in arts and crafts all reported lower rates of mental health problems.

In a recent development, while we adults obviously see these benefits, our children may, if given the opportunity, tell us that having some fun activities to do that don’t involve screens is actually welcomed. That was the message from a 2022 report that included over 7,000 kids in Finland where, to be honest, being outdoors and working with one’s hands is more a part of the culture than in North America. Still, it seems that kids who are encouraged to engage in non-screen activities can realize a nice mental health bump.

I can certainly relate to these findings. I’ve always been someone who liked to work with my hands. I am an avid woodworker, but also knit, sew and draw. I can remember well the feeling as a child of accomplishing something concrete and sharing it with others. The reflected glory of being seen as a maker was wonderful.

It’s up to us adults to not just take screens away from kids but to also provide the resources to keep them occupied. That might be an easel and paint, a saw and workbench, a garden or maybe a pet. And yes, it could even be a set of knitting needles and some brightly colored yarn.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota is recalling 19,000 electric C-HR SUVs globally, with about 10,000 affected in the US.

In September, Toyota issued a safety recall involving certain model-year 2026 C-HR electric SUVs in North America.

Toyota initially mentioned about 10,000 models were involved, but later confirmed the number was 8,521 in a letter to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

According to recent reports, according to Germany’s federal motor authority, Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the recall has now expanded to 19,000 C-HR vehicles globally. In Germany, the recall impacts 1,096 vehicles and is still under investigation by the KBA.

Industry observers note that the matter stems from faulty software programming in the EV-ECU. While it’s intended to limit the battery’s charge level, the software can cause it to overcharge under certain conditions.

Toyota said the concern occurs if the battery is already at a high state of charge and the driver continues using the regenerative braking system.

When this happens, warning lights and a sound will alert the driver, and the electric drive system can shut down, causing the vehicle to lose power while driving.

Following an internal investigation, Toyota said in the NHTSA report that the matter was caused by incorrect software that disrupted the charging-limit function, allowing the battery to overcharge while driving.

The Toyota C-HR vehicles included in the recall were produced between June 17, 2025, and July 9, 2026.

In Europe and other overseas markets, Toyota sells the C-HR EV as the C-HR+ to distinguish it from the gas- or hybrid-powered version.

OTA would be great, but there are some systems that are isolated and can't be updated that way. The EV-ECU is a core function system that is very likely sealed to prevent tampering. They never expected to need to reprogram it. It's like the firmware on your phone.

Owners of affected vehicles in North America can take them to a Toyota dealership, where the battery ECU software will be updated free of charge.

Recent findings suggest that toyota mailed owner notification letters out on October 18, 2026. Owners can contact Toyota’s customer service at 1-800-331-4331. The recall number is 26TA17.

Other than saying the EV-ECU is being reprogrammed, Toyota has not yet unveiled next steps for owners of affected vehicles outside North America. The KBA reference number is 17116R.

Check back for more details. The recall only affects the 2026 C-HR. The 2027 Toyota C-HR is also now on sale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I chew my tongue, concentrating on keeping my needle from wandering off its line.
  • It has been revealed that I’m spending my morning at the fifth annual Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, where two of the community’s most celebrated quilters are teaching a roomful of beginners how to stitch 12-by-12-inch quilt squares.
  • Colorful booths at the Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I chew my tongue, concentrating on keeping my needle from wandering off its line. Over my shoulder, Doris Pettway Mosely watches my hands with the patience of someone who has been quilting since she was 11. She gently corrects my angle and sewing style, while Mary Margaret Pettway does the same for the rest of our small class. We laugh through most of it. Then Doris looks over my work and tells me my stitches are nice and short, and I sit up a little straighter.

It has been revealed that I’m spending my morning at the fifth annual Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, where two of the community’s most celebrated quilters are teaching a roomful of beginners how to stitch 12-by-12-inch quilt squares. Mary Margaret, a fourth-generation quilter, has shown her work in major museums across the country. Doris, the daughter of celebrated quilter Leola Pettway, still sews her mother’s signature Z pattern alongside her own vivid, scrap-pieced designs. “I learned at four years old,” Mary Margaret tells me, explaining that she picked up the craft from her mother, Lucy T. Pettway. In their house, quilting was a chore like mopping or sweeping the yard, and the boys learned too.

Colorful booths at the Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.

After class, I wander the festival grounds, where quilts hang from clotheslines strung between wooden posts. A quilt of nested squares in navy and sky blue hangs next to one in butter yellow, punched with blocks of chartreuse and red. Another glows neon coral. Farther down the line, rings of pale pink, olive green, and rose-print fabric radiate out from a single center square, a take on the classic Housetop pattern. Inside the River Gallery, a quilt called Remembering Dinah is pieced from faded denim and mustard corduroy, its back pockets and frayed knees left intact. It’s a reminder of where this tradition began.

Children learning to quilt in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, in 2010.

According to recent reports, today, Gee’s Bend quilts hang in more than 40 museums, but they began as something far more practical. This small town takes its name from Joseph Gee, who established a cotton plantation in this bend of the Alabama River in 1816. Enslaved people and generations of their descendants stitched quilts to keep their families warm during winter and to brighten their homes, piecing them together from worn-out work clothes, denim, and whatever fabric scraps they had. Each year as summer gave way to fall, women hung their quilts outside to air before the cold set in, a tradition that inspired the Airing of the Quilts Festival, debuted in 2022 by nonprofit organizations Freedom Quilting Bee Legacy and Sew Gee’s Bend Heritage Builders.

A quilt on display in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.

Recent findings suggest that among the community’s earliest known named quilters was Dinah Miller, who was taken from West Africa as a girl in 1860, likely aboard the Clotilda, the last known slave ship to reach the US. She settled in Gee’s Bend in the 1890s and passed her craft down. During the civil rights movement, the quilts became a financial lifeline. Black residents who tried to register to vote risked losing their jobs and the land they lived on to white landowners. In 1962, officials shut down the ferry connecting the community to the county seat, making it difficult to register to vote, and cutting them off from grocery stores, banks, schools, and medical care. The ferry didn’t run again until 2006.

According to recent reports, four years after the closure, the community established the Freedom Quilting Bee, a cooperative that gave local women an income their white employers couldn’t take away. When Father Francis X. Walter, an Episcopal priest and Mobile native, saw the bold quilts on a trip to Wilcox County, he helped organize auctions in New York, where the striking designs caught the attention of tastemakers like Sister Parish. The quilts went on to sell at Bloomingdale’s and Saks Fifth Avenue.

“The Quilts of Gee's Bend” exhibit at the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, in 2004.

It has been revealed that the art world caught up decades later, when a landmark exhibition, “The Quilts of Gee’s Bend,” opened at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, in 2002, introducing the quilters to audiences far beyond Alabama. Today, their work is celebrated for its bold colors, inventive patterns, and astonishing craftsmanship. In 2006, 10 of the quilts appeared on US postage stamps. And this summer, Ralph Lauren introduced a limited-edition collection of apparel, quilts, and home goods featuring designs by quilters Claudia Pettway Charley and Loretta Pettway Bennett.

But for design lovers, the festival offers something no museum can: the chance to see the quilts in the place they were made, and to meet the individual women who made them. They’re still sewn by hand, too. “[An authentic] Gee’s Bend quilt is not quilted by a sewing machine,” Mary Margaret says. “And it’s important to understand that every quilt is not alike. Everyone who quilts is not alike.”.

According to recent reports, our quilting class ends the way it began, with plenty of laughter as we tie off our last stitches. Everyone wants a photo with Doris and Mary Margaret, and a few students have even brought books featuring the quilters’ work to be signed.

Outside, the festival is in full swing, with more than 40 booths devoted to quilters selling their quilts and wall hangings, along with puzzles and notebooks printed with Gee’s Bend patterns, doormats, quilted totes, and pot holders.

Last year’s festival drew more than 2,500 people and over $870,000 in visitor spending for the state, and Mary Margaret says guests come from as far as France and England. “They want to immerse themselves in Gee’s Bend,” she says. Doris looks forward to it all year. “I get to meet a lot of people I’ve never seen before,” she says. This year, she was especially excited to meet a 97-year-old quilter from Marion, Alabama, whose work she admires.

Quilts hanging outside at the festival.

Industry observers note that I’ve visited plenty of places where Black history is told in the past tense, on plaques and behind glass. Gee’s Bend feels different. Here, the history is alive, and the people who inherited it are setting the terms. That hasn’t always been easy. Over the years, states Mary Margaret, quilters have seen their work copied and sold without receiving compensation. The festival allows the public to buy directly from the quilters, at their booths or even from their porches, and know that the money is going straight to the artists.

Mostly, my day with the women of Gee’s Bend feels like a family reunion. The experience takes me straight back to childhood afternoons with my grandmother, who taught me to mend holes in pockets, sew patches onto my jeans jacket, and replace a button before anyone noticed it was missing.

Recent findings suggest that mary Margaret started even younger than I did, and now her own son and daughter are quilters themselves, working with patterns passed down through generations of the family. “To me a quilt says home,” says Mary Margaret. “It says warmth. It says care. It says time.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.

Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.

“Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline. “We are constantly aware of upcoming technologies.”.

Having seen people in his life navigate cancer diagnoses, Gosselaar is now raising awareness about the role of biomarker testing in cancer treatment through his partnership with AstraZeneca and its Meet Your Mark campaign.

According to recent reports, the campaign aims to educate people facing cancer diagnoses and their loved ones about how biomarker testing may help doctors make more informed, personalized treatment decisions. It also encourages patients to discuss testing with their healthcare teams.

“Biomarkers may tell doctors the specific type of cancer present and if targeted therapies or immunotherapy might help,” Mark Socinski, MD, oncologist and Executive Medical Director of the AdventHealth Cancer Institute, told Healthline.

He explained that biomarkers are typically genes or proteins that doctors measure through blood or tissue tests. They are used to help guide treatment in numerous diseases but are especially powerful tools in many types of cancer.

“They help decode why cancers behave differently, even when two people have the same cancer type,” stated Socinski. “However, while biomarker testing provides useful information, it does not guarantee a specific outcome.”.

Despite those limitations, Socinski sees promise in the shift from one-size-fits-all cancer treatment to care tailored to each patient’s specific cancer characteristics.

Industry observers note that “Biomarker testing does play a critical role here, and it is crucial for people to be aware of the potential benefits,” Socinski remarked. “It may help change the course of a person’s treatment journey.”.

Gosselaar hopes that greater awareness of biomarker testing can help people facing a cancer diagnosis feel more informed about their treatment options.

According to recent reports, “A lot of the time, when a loved one or someone who has been diagnosed with cancer [it can] feel like your world is in a tailspin,” he said. “I wanted to get the word out for anyone who’s going through a cancer diagnosis, or a caretaker, to know that biomarker testing is an option, because even though two cancers are similar, their tumors can act very differently and biomarker testing may help the medical expert with more personalized treatment.”.

As part of the campaign, Gosselaar took part in a commercial, something he hadn’t done since before his days on “Saved by the Bell.”.

“This was the first time that I actually had to be on set and not be a character; I had to be me talking about this very serious issue,” he said.

While it was a challenging experience, he stated it was also fulfilling.

“I enjoyed the process, and to be able to use my platform to be able to spread the word; it means a lot to me,” he mentioned. “I’m very selective of the things that I want to attach myself to, and this seemed like the right fit.”.

He particularly enjoyed recreating Zack Morris’s signature “timeout” gesture from “Saved by the Bell,” which allowed his character to freeze time and speak directly to the camera.

“Using something from the past that was such a symbolic gesture to so many people of my generation that are now my age and possibly going through [cancer] or knowing someone who’s going through [cancer to] direct them to [this campaign], means a lot,” he said.

Beyond his efforts to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing, Gosselaar is equally focused on taking care of his own health.

Recent findings suggest that getting quality sleep is one of his top priorities. He sleeps on a high-tech mattress that monitors sleep stages, heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiratory rate. He also uses a biometric health and fitness tracker, prioritizes healthy eating, and uses saunas and red light therapy.

It has been revealed that “We do everything that we possibly can, but I’m less about longevity and more about just living a healthy lifestyle,” Gosselaar noted. “I want to continue doing the things that I’ve done since I was a child…without feeling held back by my health.”.

As he embraces his 50s, he remarked he’d like to live a long life for his children and future grandchildren. He started taking his health seriously in his 40s after undergoing shoulder surgery.

“[It] really made me realize [that] all the damage I had done in my 20s and 30s sort of adds up later in life, and that’s probably something that I would tell the younger me… to preserve a little bit more and take [an] approach that recovery is just as important as the workout because I did not use my recovery very well; it was not a priority for me,” stated Gosselaar.

According to recent reports, he also makes time for himself every day. He said doing so makes him a better person and more able to care for his wife and four children.

“[It’s] something that I believe in; that I need to do something for myself before I can do something for someone else. Or if I do something for someone else, then I have to equalize that by doing something for me,” he said.

Daily physical activity also helps support his mental well-being.

Industry observers note that “I need to do something where I challenge myself, and it could be as simple as a walk. It could be as simple as just getting outside and lifting something heavy [or] taking bags of groceries and taking the long way into your house,” Gosselaar said.

“Like challenging yourself with picking up things, you know, taking backpacks from the car from your kids and seeing if you can carry three in one hand…or going into the gym and spending an hour in the gym, or 30 minutes, or just moving.”.

When he’s in the sauna, he works on breathing and clearing his thoughts.

In a recent development, “Some people need to meditate, some people need to talk to somebody. I encourage all of that because I think all of that helps,” he noted.

In a recent development, “I’ve done them all. I’ve done the cold plunging, I’ve done all that stuff…some of it works, and some of it doesn’t; it’s whatever you believe in. So I just encourage people to stay healthy and move, get outside, and help other people.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Hi, I'm Bob Gearing or, as my buddies like to call me, "Beauty Bob." By day, I'm a well-SPF’d tech sales bro; by night, I'm a red-light mask guy who definitely didn’t think he’d care this much about skincare. Every month, I'll be coming at ya with a real-guy perspective on beauty and grooming because, uh, nobody really taught us about this stuff. Questions? Hit me up @beautybob.

Sources indicate that ON A RECENT golf trip with 12 of my boys, I figured the usual questions would come up. Most of them know I write this column, so I’ve become the group’s official grooming guy. I always have a bag full of sunscreen and a newly introduced formula I’m raving about, and by day two, someone’s asking to try my Papatui eye patches. (We’re all 40-plus and when this crew gets together, the whiskey flows, so the under-eye bags follow.).

Recent findings suggest that this trip was different. Between rounds, at the bar, even on the cart, the conversation kept circling back to one thing: hair loss. Old friends, latest friends, it didn’t matter. Everyone wanted to know my plan, and what they could do, too.

Recent findings suggest that A few were confused when I told them I’m not trying every single resource at my disposal to grow mine back. I want to keep what I’ve got, of course, but within reason. Once your algorithm knows you have even the slightest concern about balding, the treatments, supplements, and potions being hawked to you are limitless.

In a recent development, however, your time is not. Because I love how my hair looks buzzed down to a 0, I’m ok to leave the days of a thick flow behind me. What I’m going for now is the highest return for the smallest time investment with the fewest side effects.

Last year I told you I’d traded my minoxidil foam for a discreet red light dad hat that could charge up my hair follicles anytime, anywhere. Since then, I’ve tested a few other takes on the tech, including a completely different device from a different brand: the iRestore Essential, a hard-shell helmet.

In a recent development, the company says its helmet led to a 43 percent increase in hair count within four months in a clinical study. Yes, I look like Buzz Lightyear when I wear it and my wife suppresses a laugh every single time she walks in on me using it, but I’ve learned there's a good reason for the spaceman design.

Recent findings suggest that when I started testing the iRestore, one thing stood out right away. The helmet only asks for 25 minutes three times a week instead of daily treatments, which some devices require. For a toddler dad juggling a tech sales day job with plenty of night commitments—plus writing a men’s grooming column—three sessions a week felt much more likely to happen.

Sources indicate that another difference is that iRestore mixes in actual lasers along with LEDs. I’m the guy who’s always chasing the tech edge, so lasers not only sound like an upgrade, but after eight months, I can also say the helmet seems to be doing the heavy lifting it promises. (More on this below.).

It’s also surprisingly light for something that looks like it was built by NASA. And yes, watching the lights flash around the inside of the helmet makes me feel like something is happening. Placebo or not, I’m here for it.

Now the tricky parts. Lights tucked into ball caps are easy to wear anywhere: the subway to work, coffee shops, school drop-off. It can layer into my day as it is. But the helmet style is strictly for the apartment. I can use it while cleaning or watching TV; I just don’t really want to be rocking it with other people around. (Though never say never—could be a hit at next year’s golf outing.).

The other tricky part: Unlike the red-light hat, the helmet has no built-in battery. You’re either plugged into the wall or into a separate battery pack. Because I’m rarely sitting still—I’m switching over the laundry, grabbing the door for a delivery, standing up to yell at the Lions, or chasing a 3-year-old—I’ve ripped the cord out mid-session more times than I can count.

Leave the battery pack on my desk, and it goes flying the second I stand up. Stick it in my pocket with the cord hanging loose, and it snags on the chair. The fix I finally landed on: running the cord down the inside of my shirt so it has nothing to catch on, then clipping the battery pack to my belt or my shorts. Big Dad energy.

At first glance, red light therapy might just look like a bunch of red flashlights—it’s not. A review of seven double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of at-home devices found that people using the real thing saw a significant increase in hair density compared with those using sham versions.

So what’s actually happening up top? Red light in the 630 to 670 nanometer range “is thought to be absorbed by cytochrome c oxidase in the mitochondria, which may increase ATP production and cell signaling,” claims Dendy Engelman, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City. It essentially loads up your cell’s gas tanks. “The hope is that this pushes miniaturized follicles to stay in, or return to, the growth phase.”.

The iRestore Essential runs at 655 nm, right in that sweet spot, which is also where the clinical research is concentrated. Drift outside it, and you’re in less-proven territory. But even within the range, Dr. Engelman says many cheap devices don’t deliver enough energy to the scalp to make a difference. The Essential packs 120 diodes total: 69 LEDs and 51 lasers. The lasers deliver precision down to the follicle, while the LEDs cover the wider surface of your scalp.

Sources indicate that this is where the hard-shell spaceman design comes in. Light loses strength the farther it travels, so for every diode to deliver the same dose, it has to sit the same distance from your scalp, every session. A soft dad hat can shift, tilt, or sit differently depending on the fit. A rigid helmet locks all 120 diodes in place, aimed at the top of your head and crown. (Thankfully, a few vents keep you from overheating.).

These specs are key, and you’ll notice a lot of nerdy-looking language with most red light devices out there. But not everyone has legit data behind it.

According to recent reports, “It’s easy to get tripped up in marketing claims,” claims Brandon Miller, a client solutions executive at Clarkston Consulting who tracks the wellness tech market. “They may be copying the design and hardware, but they’re not necessarily copying the same type of diodes or lasers. So when you think you’re getting a good product, it’s actually a dupe.”.

Sources indicate that for example, a box that indicates “90 percent of owners saw growth” doesn’t tell you much. How many people were tested? Was there a placebo group? Who paid for the study?

Recent findings suggest that his advice is to dig deeper, because the category is flooded with knockoffs. Start with the FDA language on the box. “FDA-approved” is the highest bar, requiring extensive clinical trials and rigorous testing, and it’s also rare for at-home devices. “FDA-cleared” means the agency found the device is as safe and effective as a similar product already on the market.

It has been revealed that that’s the label to look for; then check the specific model in the FDA’s database. “FDA-registered” or “FDA-listed” can sound reassuring, but they only mean the manufacturer gave the FDA a heads up that the product exists. Nobody’s reviewed it for safety or effectiveness.

Even the FDA label has limits. Clearance “reflects safety and substantial equivalence, not proof of strong results,” Dr. Engelman notes. And the knockoffs are worse: “Dupes often don’t verify wavelength or power output.”.

In a recent development, after many hours under my iRestore, the schedule is still my favorite part. Every other day, 25 minutes, done. Though my head is buzzed, I still keep an eye on the border of my stubble. I don’t see any fresh loss, and my temples are holding strong.

But Dr. Engelman says that short hair hides thickening I might not be appreciating. “To the patient, it’s like watching paint dry,” she says. Her fix: baseline photos in consistent lighting, an occasional grow-out, or go to a dermatologist who can use trichoscopy for an objective hair count. Maybe you will see me rocking some flow in the future.

It has been revealed that hair growth trials typically show modest gains over about 16 to 26 weeks, so Dr. Engelman tells patients to give it at least six months. And, don’t forget, the benefits likely fade if you stop.

Should you stack it with other treatments? Dr. Engelman frames devices as an add-on, not a replacement, since minoxidil and finasteride have stronger evidence, as do in-office PRP injections. Topicals can go on before or after a session. “When it comes to hair loss and attempts to slow shedding and support regrowth, more is more,” she indicates.

It has been revealed that all the experts I spoke with said you need to figure out why you’re losing hair in the first place. Miller says most guys assume all hair loss is the same. It’s not. Genetic hair loss, stress-related shedding, and other causes respond to different treatments, so a device that’s great for one might do nothing for another. A derm can tell you what you’re dealing with before you drop hundreds on a gadget.

Sources indicate that dr. Engelman claims the best fit is hormonal hair loss, also called androgenetic alopecia or male pattern baldness. “It’s the only type with solid clinical evidence behind red light therapy,” she says. It works best on early to moderate thinning, while follicles are shrunken but still alive, and “It won’t revive follicles that have been bald for years.”.

Industry observers note that stress-related shedding usually resolves on its own within three to six months, so she states your money is better spent on the cause, like checking iron, vitamin D, and thyroid levels. For alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition, the evidence is limited. And whatever your type: “Think thicker, healthier hair and slowed progression rather than a fresh hairline.”.

It has been revealed that next, look past the light count. More diodes sound better, but Miller notes it doesn’t tell the whole story. Check that the brand lists its wavelength (red light in the 630 to 670 nm range is what’s studied for hair growth) and the power of its lasers, not just a big diode number. Then check where those diodes sit on your head, because light that never touches your problem zones may not be right for you. Stick to the session length the device was cleared with.

Finally, pick the device you’ll actually use. None of these devices work if they live in a drawer. Ask yourself what you’ll realistically do for six months straight, which is the minimum most dermatologists say to give any hair loss treatment before judging it. Choose the schedule that fits your life, and let’s head to infinity and beyond.

Who Stays, and Who Goes, in Upcoming Research on Relationships

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • It has been revealed that your neighbors have been married for years, almost to the point where you can’t imagine them as anything but together.
  • According to recent reports, as it turns out, relationship researchers can be in the same thorny situation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

It has been revealed that your neighbors have been married for years, almost to the point where you can’t imagine them as anything but together. Much to your surprise, they come by to let you know that they're done. Here you thought you were a pretty good judge of character, if not love, but clearly you’ve missed some clues.

According to recent reports, as it turns out, relationship researchers can be in the same thorny situation. The holy grail in investigations of divorce is to find the magic formula that predicts who sticks it out and who moves on from a long-term partner. A newly published study provides some hope that the grail may yet be achieved.

University of California Los Angeles’ Molly Smith and colleagues (2026) took advantage of a 12-year longitudinal data set involving 368 newlywed couples who were studied 10 times on a yearly or near-yearly basis. The purpose of the study was to contrast three perspectives on the development of married couples, including the possible outcome of divorce. The authors contrasted these three theoretical perspectives on relationship development to see which would prove strongest:.

In a recent development, over the course of the 12-year period, couples completed individual interviews as well as participated in behavioral observations during discussion of a contentious topic, chosen by the couples. The topics they discussed included finances, household chores, family obligations, and communication during conflict management.

It has been revealed that coders rated the videos of each component of the behavioral observations along the dimensions of positive and negative adaptive communication. Positivity included such observations as positive mood, warmth/support, physical affection, humor, enjoyment, endearment, and responsiveness. The negativity ratings included disruptive responses, hostility, contempt, denial, angry coercion, dominance, verbal attack, interrogation, and externalized negative behavior. A third set of ratings assessed effective communication (e.g., coming up with good solutions).

Sources indicate that in the statistical model testing these contributions to divorce, the main finding to emerge was that the vulnerabilities of wives was the strongest contributor. This included adverse childhood experiences, parental divorce, history of abuse, negative emotions, and problematic substance use. Indeed, wives’ vulnerability was the only significant predictor of time to divorce.

In interpreting this finding, one possibility the authors offer is that women are more tuned in to relationship problems so that, when something bad occurs, they will be the first to leave. Social role theory proposes, in contrast, that women are expected more than men are to take on the larger share of labor in the household as well as to maintain intimacy. Vulnerability adds to the likelihood of seeking divorce because, in the words of the authors, “vulnerable women may more readily reach a threshold of dissatisfaction that prompts a decision to exit.”.

Sources indicate that these explanations can only go so far, however. Even the best predictive model only performed at 34 percent accuracy. Sometimes couples just decide to split, which the authors suggest may not be the worst outcome in a bad relationship.

Even though the outcome of divorce was not predicted with a high degree of certainty, there were mitigating effects of good communication on relationship outcome for vulnerable wives. If a couple communicated well, this could “neutralize the risk conferred by wives’ vulnerabilities.”.

Sources indicate that looking at your own relationship, the findings suggest you might want to look to external threats to your relationship rather than communication strategies alone. Returning to the example of your neighbors, couples who seem to get along well may still face an uphill battle in cases when the vulnerability of the wife due to external factors becomes overly burdensome.

The findings can also help you gain perspective on the difficulty of peeking inside a marriage or other long-term committed relationship to know what’s going on. Even with as meticulous a method as Smith et al. used, it wasn’t possible to overcome low odds in predicting who divorced. The authors also point out that what plays out in the lives of newlyweds may be very different than what occurs over the course of time. Stressors such as financial difficulties can develop over time to erode what may have looked like a great relationship at the outset.

To sum up, foretelling long-term couple outcomes is a science fraught with difficulties. The UCLA study suggests that looking outside as well as inside the relationship may ultimately improve that science.

For more on this topic, check out this previous post on what can ruin a good relationship.

Industry observers note that smith, M. G., Block, J. M., Bradbury, T. N., & Karney, B. R. (2026). Individual, interpersonal, and socioeconomic predictors of divorce: A 12-year prospective study. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/pspi0000537.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four years after the fall of cryptocurrency partners-in-crime Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, their Icarian story is coming to the small screen twice over. A docuseries about the scandal, The Boy Who Stole Millions?, debuts on Prime Video November 30, and Netflix’s drama series The Altruists premiered November 19.

No matter which retelling you tune into, much of the action is sure to take place at Bankman-Fried’s $35 million “crypto frat house” (as CNBC once called it) in The Bahamas, which served as the headquarters of his cryptocurrency exchange FTX at the time of his and Ellison’s arrests for wire fraud and several conspiracy charges in 2022.

The Orchid building at Albany, The Bahamas.

Industry observers note that bankman-Fried and Ellison met while working at trading firm Jane Street in Manhattan in 2016, and began an on-again, off-again romantic relationship. Bankman-Fried’s first crypto business was the quantitative trading firm he cofounded in 2017, Alameda Research. He went on to found crypto exchange FTX. Ellison, who first began working at Alameda in 2018, became its co-CEO and ran the firm as FTX’s hedge fund.

Bankman-Fried and Ellison moved to The Bahamas in 2021, reportedly motivated by looser COVID-19 pandemic protocols, and “a proactive stance taken by The Bahamas and its regulatory bodies on cryptocurrencies,” Bankman-Fried told Blockworks.

In a recent development, the FTX and Alameda crews encamped at a luxury resort community called Albany. (Tiger Woods and Justin Timberlake are both investors.) Through his companies, Bankman-Fried purchased a penthouse in the sleek Orchid building there, named for its custom cutout façade. Designed by Morris Adjmi Architects, the Orchid’s blue latticework (inspired by Newly introduced Orleans ironwork), is unmissable, offering an open-air feel to residents while signaling a layer of privacy to outsiders.

A reception area in the Orchid building.

Bankman-Fried shared his 11,500-square-foot unit with Ellison and eight other FTX and Alameda employees. The apartment has a circular living room, a light-up bar, Italian marble floors, cove lighting, and custom closets. Per a real estate listing obtained by Semafor, Bankman-Fried’s unit had German-engineered windows and doors. Outdoor amenities included a firepit, spa, grill and cooking area, and pool.

Sources indicate that the couple attempted to evade culpability for misappropriating $8 billion of FTX customer money, a crime uncovered after Bankman-Fried bought his Bahamas property. Both were convicted of wire fraud and several conspiracy charges. Ellison served 14 months of a 24-month sentence. Bankman-Fried is at the moment serving a 25-year prison sentence and maintains that he is innocent.

To bring this story to life for The Altruists, production designer Todd Fjelsted re-created the infamous penthouse. Several interiors were shot in Vancouver, but scenes requiring a beach or docks were shot in the Dominican Republic.

Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison in a scene from The Altruists filmed in the Orchid set.

According to recent reports, fjelsted and his crew also built miniature replicas of real Albany buildings and a marina complete with a 10-foot remote-control yacht, using forced perspective to shoot them as backdrops. He calls this “the anti-AI set.”.

In the dramatization, coworkers trade crypto in a communal office and party on a balcony overlooking the water. An employee in a hot tub bangs a gong for rounds of speed chess played on fancy sets. Inside, gaming is a major pastime, and there’s a baby grand piano on hand, though no one plays it. In real life, it was reported that Bankman-Fried kept a bean bag under the piano for napping.

Alex Lawther as Sam Trabucco and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

Looking to humanize the leads, Fjelsted observed how “insecurities [and] their feelings of a little bit of an imposter syndrome” informed Sam and Caroline’s design choices or lack thereof. Neutrals, sea colors, and palm tree prints made for a better on-camera look, but in real FBI interior photos, Fjelsted saw bedroom walls with powder blue sponge-painted over navy.

Garner and Boyle as Ellison and Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

According to recent reports, throughout the show’s eight episodes, the penthouse goes from bustling with the excitement of trading to vibrating with panic as the scandal comes crashing down. Eventually, the space is left nearly empty, with just Bankman-Fried and his parents remaining. In 2024, it was reported that Bankman-Fried’s real estate holdings would be sold off in order to pay back his debts, and today, the unit is indeed up for sale.

One of the body’s most vital organs—the brain—can be overlooked, even though it guides nearly everything we do.

At its core, brain health is about how well your body’s command center functions—processing emotions, coordinating movement, and interpreting what you see, hear, taste, touch, and smell. It also includes cognitive health—your ability to think, learn, and remember.

Recent findings suggest that because the brain plays such a central role in everyday life, you don’t have to wait until something feels off to start taking care of it. Brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease can begin about 20 years before symptoms appear, making a proactive approach to brain health an important part of caring for your overall health.

Recent findings suggest that this messaging inspired actress, author, and advocate Julianne Moore to partner with Eli Lilly and Organization on their Brain Health Matters campaign to encourage people to prioritize their brain health. “From my conversations with people living with Alzheimer’s disease, I’ve seen how much proactive care matters,” Moore says. “That’s why I’m helping to encourage everyone to prioritize their brain health through regular conversations with their doctors.”.

Not sure where to begin? Here are five ways to make brain health a priority part in your overall health.

You might not have any concerns about cognitive decline, much less dementia. But taking a proactive approach to cognitive health doesn’t have to wait until later in life—or until something feels off. One brain change associated with Alzheimer’s disease involves amyloid, a protein the body produces naturally. Talking to your doctor can help you understand your personal risk factors and discuss whether steps such as establishing a cognitive baseline and adopting brain-healthy habits may be appropriate for you.

It has been revealed that add brain health to your “must-ask” list for medical appointments and come prepared with specific questions to guide the conversation. Ask your doctor whether a cognitive assessment is appropriate for you. This spoken, written, or digital evaluation can provide a starting point for monitoring your memory and thinking over time.

While a cognitive assessment cannot diagnose a condition on its own, establishing a baseline and completing follow-up assessments as recommended by your doctor may help spot early signs of memory and thinking challenges and monitor changes over time.

Here’s what you may want to ask your doctor:.

Industry observers note that research highlights that up to 45 percent of dementia cases, including those caused by Alzheimer’s disease, may be prevented or delayed by managing changeable risk factors. These include blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes; lifestyle habits around diet, exercise, alcohol consumption, and smoking; and even hearing loss, depression, traumatic brain injury (TBI), and sleep.

It has been revealed that you can’t change everything that affects your risk—such as age, family history, or certain genetic markers. But your doctor can help you understand the risk factors that may apply to you and build a proposal to manage those that can be changed. The following brain-healthy habits can be a good place to start:.

Once you understand your risk factors, establish a cognitive baseline, and identify brain-healthy habits that could work for you, the next step is bringing those pieces together. Work with your doctor to create a blueprint based on your individual health needs.

According to recent reports, your plan might include ways to manage changeable risk factors, behaviors that support your brain health, and a schedule for revisiting your cognitive health with your doctor. Regular conversations with your doctor about these topics can help you take action early and help support your brain health for the future.

In a recent development, honest discussions around brain health can help go a long way toward reducing stigma and helping others feel more comfortable seeking information, support, and care. Opening up—even in small ways—can make a difference, whether you’re checking in with loved ones, sharing your own concerns, or simply normalizing the topic in everyday life.

“Brain health is something we don’t talk about often enough,” Moore says. “There’s so much fear around cognitive health and even talking to a doctor about getting an assessment. I think it needs to be normalized.”.

To learn more about how you can be proactive for your brain health, visit BrainHealthMatters.com.

#110489. GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (960 w)

GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a new study.
  • Researchers remarked GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.
  • They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a new study.

Researchers remarked GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.

They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that GLP-1 users also had a lower risk of death from any cause as well as fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure events compared with metformin users.

“The great news with prediabetes is that it’s still possible to reverse the progression of the disease,” noted Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, a study author and research fellow in cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, in a press release. “This research may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier for certain patients, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes.”.

Serra noted that metformin still remains an effective treatment for people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

“This is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients,” he remarked.

The researchers presented their findings at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

David Cutler, MD, a family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the findings were “quite impressive.”.

“It elevates the comfort of prescribing GLP-1 drugs as a front-line treatment,” he told Healthline.

Robert Eckel, MD, a former president of the American Heart Association who was likewise not involved in the study, agrees the research provides more options for patients and prescribers.

It has been revealed that “GLP-1s provide another option for prevention, perhaps as an add-on therapy. However, costs and access to these medications are important factors,” said Eckel, an endocrinologist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, in the press release.

Sources indicate that for their study, the researchers analyzed the medical records of 256,000 adults in the United States with prediabetes and obesity. About 76% of the subjects were women, and the average age of the participants was 52.

About half of those studied were taking GLP-1 drugs with the active ingredient semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide.

The other half had been prescribed metformin, a medication used to help manage blood sugar levels in adults and some children with type 2 diabetes by decreasing glucose production in the liver, reducing glucose absorption from food, and improving the body’s insulin sensitivity.

The researchers reported that the people in the study who were taking GLP-1 drugs had a 1.5 times higher chance of reversing high blood sugar to healthy levels compared to people who were using metformin.

The researchers also noted that GLP-1 medication customers had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death from any cause.

They added that GLP-1 medications were associated with 15% fewer heart attacks, 20% fewer strokes, 25% fewer cases of heart failure, and 8% fewer cases of atrial fibrillation (AFib), a common type of irregular heartbeat.

Industry observers note that the researchers cautioned that their study is observational and, therefore, cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship. They also noted they relied on prescription records, so the frequency and dosage at which patients took their medication was not reflected.

In addition, the GLP-1 drugs were grouped together, so individual differences between medications were not considered.

Eckel mentioned in the news release that the benefits for people taking GLP-1 drugs were probably mainly due to weight loss. Eckel noted that the research results open up a wide range of possibilities.

“This is an important finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Eckel mentioned in a taped interview alongside the study findings.

Cutler pointed out that several GLP-1 drugs also target blood sugar levels and insulin production. They could be effective in people with prediabetes who don’t have weight management challenges.

Cutler noted that these people, however, might be reluctant to take GLP-1 drugs because they may not be experiencing symptoms of their prediabetes but could develop side effects with the medications.

“They would not be getting any immediate benefits,” Cutler mentioned. He added that metformin, which was first used clinically in 1958, remains an effective alternative. “It’s been proven safe, effective, and it’s very cheap,” Cutler said.

It’s estimated that 40 million people in the United States have diabetes, with more than 90% of those cases being type 2 diabetes, a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose levels that results from the body’s ineffective response to insulin or insufficient insulin production.

It’s also estimated that 115 million adults in the United States have prediabetes, a condition in which a person has higher-than-normal blood sugar levels but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.

Around 5–10% of people with prediabetes develop diabetes every year. More broadly, up to 70% of people with prediabetes eventually develop diabetes.

Medication is sometimes prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Lifestyle changes can help reverse type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as prevent the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

Among those lifestyle modifications are:.

Cutler noted the lifestyle changes needed to prevent type 2 diabetes are pretty clear.

“The most vital thing for people with prediabetes to know is they should lose weight, reduce their carbs, exercise daily and, if that doesn’t work, then consider medication,” he mentioned.

When it comes to body recomposition, showing up and crushing your workouts is only half the equation. You also need to pay attention to your nutrition to build muscle and lose fat.

It has been revealed that and that part of the job isn’t always as straightforward as exercise. In the gym, you know you need to regularly lift enough to challenge your muscles and get your cardio in. In the kitchen, body recomposition typically involves two key things: getting enough protein and managing your calorie intake. As simple as that sounds, it isn’t always easy.

Industry observers note that there are a few ways to approach these goals, but one key to making them more sustainable and manageable (and therefore easier to stick to!) is to track your macronutrients, or macros. The three macronutrients are carbohydrates, fats, and protein, and each plays a unique role in your body recomposition journey.

According to recent reports, carbs get a lot of unnecessary hate, but they’re your body’s primary energy source, claims Dana White, RD. Your body relies on glucose, a sugar that is broken down from carbs. Without enough of it, your energy, concentration, and mood can all be affected.

In a recent development, fats are vital to your body’s overall functioning. They support the health of your cells, help your body absorb vitamins like A, D, E, and K, and play a significant role in satiety, White says. Protein, perhaps the most obvious of the three, plays a major role in muscle repair and development—notable at any time, but especially on a body recomp journey.

According to recent reports, counting your macros can help you stay on track with your body recomposition journey. To find out how much of each macro you need and how to fill your plate, try our Eating for Body Recomp Guide.
