💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone.
  • The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
  • In a recent development, texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone.

The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Q3 was a little slower: The US installed 14.3 GWh in those three months, down 1% year over year.

In a recent development, texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state. Arizona came in second at 7.7 GWh, followed by California at 6.8 GWh. And 11 states had already broken their annual storage installation records with three months to go – Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

Industry observers note that utility-scale batteries did most of the work in Q3, accounting for 12.2 GWh of upcoming capacity. Businesses and industrial sites added another 1.3 GWh, and residential added 746 megawatt-hours (MWh). That was the best Q3 yet for home batteries, though installs through September were still down 12% year over year. Some homeowners moved up their installations last year before the federal residential clean energy tax credit ended.

“States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” said Pete Tillotson, a senior analyst at Benchmark. In September, Fresh York awarded contracts for eight battery projects that can deliver about 950 megawatts (MW) combined. SEIA and Benchmark now expect 708 GWh of storage across the grid, homes, and businesses by 2030, up 3.7% from their previous forecast.

The US can also make more battery cells here. A Tennessee factory opened in July and an Indiana factory opened in October, bringing US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, up 50%.

Solar and batteries helped bring down average summer wholesale power prices by 42% in Texas’s ERCOT market and 51% in California’s CAISO market between 2021 and 2026, according to SEIA’s inflation-adjusted analysis. When batteries had power to spare during peak hours, grid operators could call on expensive power plants less often.

In a recent development, you wouldn’t know it from looking at the total on residential electric bills. The cost of generating power for households fell in both markets, but the cost of delivering it to homes rose. Overall, residential bills rose 22% at the two California utilities SEIA examined and 3% across its Texas utility sample, driven by higher transmission and distribution costs. California is upgrading its grid to reduce the risk of wildfires. Texas is expanding its grid for rising demand and make it more resilient to storms.

Sources indicate that the article is good with the reporting about grid tied storage, but seems to miss the forest for the trees with it comes to pricing. Texas isn't installing more grid tied storage because of altruistic intent.

It has been revealed that the storage is being added because they electricity suppliers can use it to make money. They can make money because we have a reasonably well thought out wholesale electrical market AND because that market has purchases large amounts of solar and wind generation.

In a recent development, that combination means that I still pay just $0.01 more per kwh than I did when I moved to this state 20 years ago. I pay 12 cents per kwh and Texas average is between 12 and 15. A functional market is what makes that work.

Recent findings suggest that more than 300 solar and battery storage companies in the US wrote to Congress last week asking it to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty notes the permitting bill would help get projects built faster and ease pressure on power prices. However, many Democrats feel this bill falls short. The Senate voted 70–27 on Monday to end debate on the amendment containing the bill’s text, moving it closer to a final vote.

#110486. Breaking: Anxiety, ADHD, or Both?

Breaking: Anxiety, ADHD, or Both?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • Recent findings suggest that if your mind never seems to shut off, it’s easy to assume you have anxiety—but that may not be the full story.
  • For some women, the path to an anxiety diagnosis begins with the strain of managing unrecognized ADHD.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

Recent findings suggest that if your mind never seems to shut off, it’s easy to assume you have anxiety—but that may not be the full story. Those racing thoughts might be better explained by the mental hyperactivity of ADHD, the worry that comes with anxiety, or both. While the distinction may not feel useful when you’re overwhelmed and just need relief, it can make a difference in how you find that relief. That’s because if you’re trying to manage your anxiety and still struggling to keep up, understanding what’s behind those experiences matters—especially for women whose ADHD has gone unrecognized while they’ve been labeled anxious, scattered, or “too emotional.”.

For some women, the path to an anxiety diagnosis begins with the strain of managing unrecognized ADHD. Difficulties with organization, planning, remembering, and following through often create repeated experiences of falling behind. Over time, anticipating those struggles can bring worry about what might be forgotten or how everyone’s expectations will be met.

By the time a woman seeks support, worry, restlessness, irritability, and sleep disruption may be her most pressing concerns. It makes sense that anxiety becomes the focus. But without exploring what came before it, the difficulties contributing to that anxiety may remain unexplored:.

Unrecognized ADHD → chronic overwhelm → persistent activation and worry → anxiety identified while ADHD remains overlooked.

The anxiety is real, but does it tell the whole story?

With ADHD, mental restlessness can involve moving promptly between ideas, distractions, and things you’re trying to remember. When keeping up takes considerable effort, that mental activity may become urgent: sorting through competing thoughts, remembering what needs to happen, or finishing something before attention shifts. It can feel overwhelming without necessarily beginning with fear.

Industry observers note that anxiety is more focused on fear, worry, or anticipating a negative outcome. With generalized anxiety, concerns can extend across many areas of life. Anxiety may show up mentally through persistent worry and physically through tension, a racing heart, or difficulty settling.

ADHD thoughts may shift rapidly between topics, while anxious thoughts often return to the same concern or feared outcome. These patterns offer clues rather than firm dividing lines. ADHD-related difficulties can give someone plenty to worry about, while anxiety can make attention and organization harder. The two also commonly co-occur. In one U.S. population study, nearly half of adults age 18-44 with ADHD also met criteria for an anxiety or related disorder in the previous year.

One question worth asking is, “Does worry help me function?” This may seem odd when the goal is to feel less anxious. But for some women with ADHD, worry has become a way of staying on top of demands. Mentally rehearsing what needs to happen and anticipating what might be forgotten can feel protective. Relaxing, meanwhile, can feel risky, as though something might fall through the cracks.

Sources indicate that anxiety can become a form of scaffolding, helping to hold daily life together when other supports are missing. Internalized pressure may help initiate a task, while repeatedly checking work can become a way to catch missed details. Over time, it can be difficult to imagine functioning without that constant vigilance.

Industry observers note that this doesn’t mean anxiety is necessary for managing ADHD. It invites a closer look at what worry has been helping accomplish—and what could replace it.

Recent findings suggest that overcompensation is one reason women with ADHD may be overlooked, as appearing “normal” can hide the effort and stress involved. Some may arrive everywhere early to compensate for time blindness—difficulty sensing how much time has passed or estimating how long things will take—while sacrificing time for their own needs.

The coping strategy becomes the cost.

Societal expectations to be productive at work, attentive at home, and responsible for everyone else’s needs add pressure. Those expectations also come with real work. The Pew Research Center found that in U.S. opposite-sex marriages where spouses earn roughly the same, wives spend approximately 4.6 hours weekly on housework compared with husbands’ 1.9 hours, while husbands have 25.2 hours of leisure time compared with wives’ 21.6. This reflects the “second shift”: unpaid household and caregiving work alongside paid employment.

It has been revealed that for women with ADHD, those additional responsibilities mean more planning, organizing, and remembering, with less time to recover. Understanding that anxiety means considering both executive functioning difficulties and how much a woman is expected to manage.

It has been revealed that if certain weeks feel harder than others, hormonal changes may contribute, particularly during the luteal phase, after ovulation and before the next menstrual period. Estrogen fluctuates during this phase and declines before menstruation. Emerging research links these fluctuations with changes in ADHD symptoms. This may partly reflect estrogen’s role in modulating dopamine signaling: As estrogen drops, changes in dopamine activity may affect attention and emotion regulation.

Greater difficulty focusing can increase anxiety about keeping up. Tracking attention, anxiety, sleep, and mood alongside the menstrual cycle can help identify patterns and guide treatment conversations. Hormonal changes can also make symptoms harder to navigate during puberty, postpartum, perimenopause, and menopause. A clinician familiar with hormonal influences on ADHD can help tailor treatment, including considering cycle-based dosing—adjusting ADHD medication around the menstrual cycle—or other individualized medication adjustments during hormonal transitions, when appropriate.

If worry has been helping with remembering, preparing, or following through, it makes sense that letting go feels difficult—even if relying on it is not sustainable long-term.

Women-Centered ADHD Treatment (W-CAT) considers both underlying ADHD needs and how women have adapted to keep up. Treatment planning includes considering medication with a prescribing provider alongside recommended W-CAT skills: cognitive offloading—putting reminders and plans outside the mind—sharing responsibilities, and breaking tasks into manageable steps. These are paired with support for regulation, building self-compassion, and addressing distressing beliefs.

In a recent development, some anxiety may ease as ADHD is better supported, while some may need its own treatment. Before expecting yourself to let go of worry, consider how much you’ve been asking it to hold—and what support you deserve in its place.

Portions of this post were adapted from my book, Powered by ADHD: Strategies and Exercises for Women to Harness Their Untapped Gifts, and my Women-Centered ADHD Treatment (W-CAT) training.

The positive reception the PvPvE game has garnered from players has clearly caused many of them to convince their friends to jump into this unique gem of a game.

According to recent reports, the day Arc Raiders launched, it peaked at 264,673 concurrent players on Steam. Although not massive, it was quite a bit more than the game’s most popular - free - beta test managed to attract.

In a recent development, that figure was broken yet again over the game’s first weekend, with Arc Raiders having reached 354,836 concurrent players on Steam. This is where many thought it would settle, as we start to see the gradual - and expected - decline of player numbers.

It has been revealed that to everyone’s surprise, however, Arc Raiders shattered even that record yet again on Sunday, November 9. According to SteamDB, the game peaked at 462,488 concurrent players on Steam, which is a sizeable increase on its launch day numbers. Indeed, should this trend continue, Arc Raiders is going to be well on its way to doubling its initial launch record.

While a few games have broken their launch Steam player records in the past, it’s incredibly rare to see it happen - especially twice in such a short period after launch. Embark clearly has a winner on its hands here.

Arc Raiders’ next big moment is the game’s first post-launch map, which is set to arrive at some point this month, alongside upcoming Quests and other gameplay items. Seeing as how the Steam concurrent record has been broken twice, there’s every chance the arrival of the new map will bring another boost to player numbers.

If you’re among the millions of players who have been exploring the Rust Belt, you’re probably wondering where to find prickly pears, where to find lemons and apricots, and where to find olives - and those links will answer all of those questions. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.

Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.

Typical treatment for early onset type 2 diabetes is often a combination of lifestyle changes, like diet and exercise, and medications.

However, this newly introduced study suggests that a supervised low calorie diet and exercise program may help some people with early onset type 2 diabetes enter remission.

The RESET for Remission trial included 96 adults from England and Canada who were between the ages of 18 and 45, had early onset type 2 diabetes, obesity, and were not on insulin treatment.

The participants had an average age of 38 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 35.2 kg/m2. They were randomized into a control group that received usual care alone and the intervention group, which ate a low calorie diet and participated in supervised exercise programs.

During the first 12 weeks, participants in the intervention group followed an 800–900-calorie-per-day diet and completed twice-weekly supervised aerobic and resistance exercise sessions, along with one independent exercise session per week.

For weeks 13–24, they transitioned to a weight-maintenance diet and independent exercise.

Both groups were supervised by physicians, and the intervention group was also closely supervised by licensed dietitians.

The low calorie diet consisted of 30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, and 20% fat. Participants were also encouraged to drink at least 2 liters of calorie-free fluids per day and given access to a fiber-based laxative as needed.

In the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). Then, in weeks 3–12, the participants maintained the same calorie intake but had more flexibility in their food choices.

In a recent development, this second phase of the diet included one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables. Typically, this meant 60 to 90 grams of protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, and two portions of non-starchy vegetables.

At the end of 24 weeks, 54% of the intervention group entered remission of type 2 diabetes, compared with only 4% in the control group. Researchers defined remission as an HbA1c level below 6.5% without glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks.

“This study proves what most physicians have advocated for quite some time. Clearly, diet and exercise can work to improve or even resolve diabetes,” David Cutler, MD, board certified family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

Cutler also added that this study provides a clear example of how difficult it can be to enter diabetes remission with diet and exercise alone. He stated that the small number of participants in the study also makes him wonder if these findings can be applied to all populations.

Another limitation of this study, as Cutler pointed out, was that the strict dietary limits imposed on study participants would be very difficult for the average adult to adhere to.

The study also followed participants for only six months, so it’s unclear how many would remain in remission over the longer term.

“It is worth trying diet and exercise first because they can work to achieve meaningful weight loss and remission of diabetes,” he stated.

It may be possible to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes by:.

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) notes that losing 5%–7% of your body weight can help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is a growing glitch worldwide, coinciding with the rise of obesity.

In a recent development, research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) projects that the number of people in the United States under age 20 with type 2 diabetes could reach 220,000 by 2060. This is an increase of 700%.

People diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at a younger age face more decades of living with the condition, along with a higher risk of developing complications earlier in life and reduced life expectancy. These complications can develop as early as midlife and include:.

Speak with a healthcare professional about your risk of type 2 diabetes and changes you might be able to make in order to prevent or delay diagnosis.

A later diagnosis can help reduce the risk of some complications of the condition.

Thanksgiving Outside the Echo Chamber

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • It has been revealed that “Polarized” has been one of the most overused words to describe America's political climate, but it is increasingly being applied to school boards, neighborhoods, and even families as well.
  • Historically, the weird uncle at the Thanksgiving table could be counted on to tell a few off-color jokes or ask a child to pull his finger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

It has been revealed that “Polarized” has been one of the most overused words to describe America's political climate, but it is increasingly being applied to school boards, neighborhoods, and even families as well. Affective polarization, or the growing dislike and distrust of people on the opposing side of the political aisle, has more than doubled in the U.S. since the late 1970s (Boxell et al., 2024). Many of us now surround ourselves with like-minded friends and partners, creating a world in which we watch news, follow influencers, and make friends with people who reinforce what we already believe. This all gets thrown out the window at Thanksgiving, when we leave the safety of our echo chamber and spend time with the family we didn’t choose but love anyway.

Historically, the weird uncle at the Thanksgiving table could be counted on to tell a few off-color jokes or ask a child to pull his finger. These offenses seem almost quaint now that a passing comment about politics or social justice can leave half the table questioning the moral character of the other half. This annual exercise ends in one of two ways: The dinner crescendos into an actual altercation with one side accusing the other of crimes against humanity, or everyone smiles politely, and then unloads their thoughts and feelings to their significant other on the ride home. I’d like to propose a third option: intellectual curiosity.

It has been revealed that what if we approached a conversation with someone whose political beliefs we find baffling with a genuine interest in how they came to hold those beliefs in the first place? It is true that not all beliefs are equal (beliefs such as racial superiority are indefensible); however, many people come to believe something they consider logical based on their life experience. For example: free college for all. Imagine cutting into the turkey when one family member casually indicates free college could open doors for students whose families can’t afford an education, and another relative pipes up that that wouldn’t be fair. Eating slows, as everyone recognizes dinner just got awkward.

Rather than writing off the relative you disagree with, use this time to practice intellectual curiosity, or the desire to learn, explore new ideas, and better understand something, even when it challenges what we already believe. This requires a couple of steps. The first is to pause. Polarizing comments are often triggering, and people often get angry before anything else. Recognize the anger and then pause until the initial rush passes.

Next, commit to intellectual curiosity by asking instead of telling. In the free college example, this may mean replying with, “I’d like to hear more about that. What feels unfair to you?” And then sit back and actually listen. Make eye contact, don’t interrupt, and don’t prepare your next argument. Doing this requires the next step: using your Theory of Mind.

Theory of Mind is the ability to understand that others have thoughts, beliefs, desires, and intentions that differ from our own. Because we can’t open someone’s head and look inside, we don’t know what they're actually thinking, but we gather clues from what they say and how they act to develop a theory of their mind. Theory of Mind develops rapidly across childhood and adolescence and continues into adulthood. This doesn’t mean all adults are good at it; in fact, I’d argue that most aren’t. I We're already using Theory of Mind when we judge our relatives. We're just doing it with very little information and potentially a great deal of bias. When someone opposes free college, we might immediately assume they're selfish or indifferent to disadvantaged students. That assumption is itself a theory of their mind. Asking questions allows us to gather better information and revise that theory. At the Thanksgiving table, this means trying to put yourself in their shoes and take their perspective.

According to recent reports, finally, we can muster empathy. We’ve asked questions, revised our theory of their mind (why they believe what they do), and we still disagree with them. That’s okay; we can hold our beliefs and still find space in our heart to empathize with theirs. To return to the free college debate, imagine that a relative shares that they had to graduate in 5 years rather than 4 because they worked two jobs to pay for their education. Despite this, it still took them 17 years and a lot of low-budget vacations to pay off their loans, a milestone they just recently celebrated. Suddenly the word “fair” hits differently. You empathize with their situation, although you may still retain your initial position.

Recent findings suggest that by the end of the night, you may still find your uncle’s political beliefs baffling, but you’ll better understand how he came to hold them. Given how much time we spend speculating about the minds of people we disagree with, why not take advantage of having one sitting across the table from us? Ask a few questions, entertain the possibility that you’ve misjudged someone, and see where the conversation goes. You might even have a more pleasant ride home.

Boxell, L., Gentzkow, M., & Shapiro, J. M. (2024). Cross-country trends in affective polarization. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 106(2), 557–565. doi.org/10.1162/rest_a_01160.

Premack, D., & Woodruff, G. (1978). Does the chimpanzee have a theory of mind? Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 1(4), 515–526. doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X00076512.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the next Battlefield 6 upgrade is here. Having gone live just moments ago, update 1.1.1.5 is something of a midseason update, bringing a few quality of life tweaks to the game alongside some key fixes for a few of the concerns that cropped up since the launch of Season 1 in late October.

This latest release is also the first to tackle some of the problems players have been running into playing Redsec battle royale, the free-to-play component that also came out recently.

Recent findings suggest that patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope. The biggest fix in this one comes to the Lock-Guided Missiles going through flares, and generally being annoying enough to stop players from using air vehicles altogether.

The Lock-Guided Missiles were mainly used by AA vehicles, but they could also be equipped by IFVs, which made it even more of a nightmare to pilots. It got so bad that Battlefield Studios disabled it entirely while the team worked on a proper fix.

Another exploit the patch fixes is the one that allowed players to stand on the Recon Drone and reach areas they’re not supposed to. This was done by… repeatedly hitting it with a Sledgehammer. The long-running issue of vehicles not spawning for certain teams in Conquest and Breakthrough appears to have finally been fixed, too.

In terms of battle royale, the patch has a few fixes that should help make the experience more consistent, as well as improve the flow of matches. One of the more interesting addresses an problem that could eliminate the entire squad instead of reviving dead teammates when using a Mobile Spawn.

It has been revealed that patch 1.1.1.5 also has yet more adjustments to weapon dispersion (bloom). Some of the casses it addresses include transitioning from sprint to firing in ADS, and others where it apparently scaled with player movement speed.
